Everyone uses the same AI Instance provider, All
Only certain people Instance provider, Selected people, enable them under Users
Everyone with their own solution No provider (or one as well), People may add their own provider/key
All settings can also be preset with environment variables, for instance for automated installations. They apply until someone saves in the administration.

en.heading: Close pages and spaces to AI
paragraphs: Owners of a workspace or a space can mark a page (under Share → People) or a space (in the space settings) Closed to AI. This applies to everyone and to everything below – sub-pages and database records. No AI feature reads this content, even if a person allowed it in their own rules.
New contacts databases start closed to the AI; whoever manages the page can open them.

en.heading: For users
paragraphs: Under Settings → AI:
– Provider in use: which provider works for you and whether your text leaves the server ("Your text is processed on this server and does not leave it." with Ollama).
– Use AI features: switch AI off for yourself entirely – or single features.
– On this device (Apple): whether Apple Intelligence is available here and whether Flowplan should use it – When possible (default), Only without AI on the server or Off (on-device AI).

– Set up own provider (if administrators allow it): provider, address, model and your key. Your own providers need public https addresses. If there is an instance provider too, choose under Which provider to use between The instance's and My own.

en.heading: What the AI may access
paragraphs: You decide which content the AI may read:
– Everything I may see (default) – with exceptions you exclude.
– Only selected – only workspaces, spaces, pages and databases you allow.

With Add rule you pick a workspace, space, page or database and allow or exclude it. Rules apply to sub-pages and records too; the closest rule wins. For example, allow a whole workspace and exclude a page with salary data in it.
The AI never reads:
– pages and records you may not see,
– other people's private records,
– the trash,
– journals with a PIN lock (even when unlocked),
– pages and spaces closed to AI.
On a page the AI may not read, AI features are greyed out with a note saying why.

en.heading: Security of keys
paragraphs: – Stored encrypted: API keys – the instance's and everyone's – are only stored encrypted in the database (AES-256-GCM, bound to their owner; a copied value can't be decrypted elsewhere). The key for this comes from FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY or the file secrets.key in the data folder (Stored secrets).
– Write-only: a stored key is never shown again – not in the interface, the API, exports, backups or logs. Only "stored · ends in …abcd" with Replace and Remove is visible.

– Bound to the address: if the provider or address changes, the stored key is deleted. A key therefore never goes to a server other than the one it was entered for. Keys are only sent in headers, never in addresses; redirects are not followed.
– No internal addresses for own providers: people's own providers only reach public https addresses – no addresses in the internal network or of the server itself.
– From environment variables: a key from FLOWPLAN_AI_API_KEY is never stored in the database and only used for the provider from the variables.
– Error messages from providers are cleaned of keys before they are shown or logged.

– No access with API tokens or in the demo: API tokens can neither read nor change AI settings and cannot use AI features; in the demo, AI through the server is off (on-device AI is there with the default settings).
– Limits: at most 30 requests per minute, 300 per hour (FLOWPLAN_AI_REQUESTS_PER_HOUR) and 3 at once per person.

– Backups: secrets.key is not part of the instance backup. After restoring on another server without this file, Flowplan shows "stored but unreadable – please replace", and the keys are entered again.

en.heading: Frequently asked questions
paragraphs: Do I have to use AI? No. AI through the server is off until administrators switch it on, and everyone can switch it off for themselves. AI on Apple devices is allowed because the text does not leave the device, and it is just as optional: Settings → AI → On this device (Apple) → Off.
Does anything go to the server with on-device AI? No. The text is processed on the iPhone, iPad or Mac; the server only learns which setting you chose.
Does it work without any cloud? Yes, with Ollama on your own server. Then no text leaves the server.
Does the provider train on my data? That depends on the provider's terms. Flowplan only sends what a request needs, and only content the AI may read. If you want to be sure, use Ollama.
Are conversations stored? Flowplan does not keep requests and answers permanently; whatever you insert into pages is normal content with version history.
Can the AI change things by itself? No. AI actions are proposals; only when you select them and press Run are they created with your permissions.
What about the MCP server? The MCP server is a different route: an external assistant such as Claude Desktop works with your Flowplan. It is independent of the settings here.
With personal API tokens, scripts, n8n or Home Assistant access Flowplan; webhooks report new records, form answers and pages to other services.

en.heading: API tokens
paragraphs: Under Settings → API & AI assistants you create tokens: with a name, Read only, Read and write or Browser extension only. The token is shown only once – afterwards only its beginning is visible. A Read only token is refused for every request that writes, including restoring backups and uploading files.
– Browser extension only: for the browser extension. The token only reaches /api/clipper/targets and /api/clipper/save; everywhere else it counts as no token.
Every request with the token acts with your permissions:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer fp_…" https://flowplan.example.com/api/bootstrap

– Read: all GET endpoints, such as /api/bootstrap (workspace, pages) and /api/pages/ (a document, or a database with its records). In a database's answer the records are under rows (with preview instead of the full document); related contains linked databases, the database's own records are only under rows.
– Write: POST /api/command with the same action as the interface, e.g. to create a record:
curl -X POST https://flowplan.example.com/api/command \
-H "Authorization: Bearer fp_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"action":"row.create","pageId":"<database ID>","cells":{"title":"From Home Assistant"}}'
Markdown export also works with a read token, since it only reads – e.g. for a cron job that pushes the export into a Git repository (or let Flowplan do it, see Markdown export and Git):
curl -sf -X POST https://flowplan.example.com/api/markdown-export \
-H "Authorization: Bearer fp_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"pageId":"<page id>","format":"zip","includeSubpages":true,"history":true}' -o export.zip
Instead of pageId, spaceId exports a whole space into one ZIP: {"spaceId":"","format":"zip","history":true}.

Block links: GET /api/pages/{pageId}/blocks/{blockId} returns the title and the start of a block's text (with ?row= for records), GET /api/blocks?workspace=…&q=… searches headings and blocks, and the block.ids action gives the blocks of an older document their ids.
Tokens never get administrator rights and cannot create further tokens. You can revoke them at any time in the same list; locked accounts lose their tokens automatically.
To connect Claude, ChatGPT or other AI assistants, use the MCP server with a token like this.

en.heading: Idempotency-Key: retries without doubles
paragraphs: A request can fail without an answer – the connection drops, a proxy times out – although Flowplan already applied it. So that a script can simply try again, every changing request takes the header Idempotency-Key: one key per logical action (e.g. a UUID v4, 8–128 characters of A–Z a–z 0–9 _ -), sent again unchanged with every retry of that action.
KEY=$(uuidgen)
curl -X POST https://flowplan.example.com/api/command \
-H "Authorization: Bearer fp_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "Idempotency-Key: $KEY" \
-d '{"action":"comment.create","pageId":"<page ID>","body":"Deployed"}'
# The same request with the same key again: no second comment.
– First request: applied; the key is stored with the answer. For POST /api/command this happens in the same transaction as the change – either both or neither.
– Same key, same request (method, path and body): the stored answer with the same status, marked with Idempotent-Replayed: true. Nothing is applied again.
– Same key, different request: 422 (code: idempotency_key_reused).
– First request still running: 409 with Retry-After (code: idempotency_in_progress) – wait and send again with the same key.

– Answers with secrets (a new API token, a feed address, an access password) and answers larger than 64 KB are not stored: a repeat gets 409 (code: idempotency_already_applied) instead of the secret a second time.
– An invalid key gives 400 (code: idempotency_key_invalid). A failed request (4xx, 5xx) keeps no key – after fixing the cause it can be sent again with the same key.

Keys belong to whoever sends them: to the person for the web app, to the API token, or to the app installation (widgets, Shortcuts, share sheet). The same key of another token or person is a different key. Keys expire after 24 hours. Requests without the header work as before.

The header is accepted by POST /api/command, uploads (/api/upload), imports, webhooks, time reports, issue sync, the browser extension's /api/clipper/save and the actions of the mobile apps; the OpenAPI document marks these operations (x-idempotent). The web app, the mobile apps (widgets, Shortcuts, share sheet, notification buttons, changes queued offline) and the generated SDKs send a key with every change on their own and keep it when they retry – a double click, a tap with a weak signal or a reconnect never applies a change twice.

en.heading: Webhooks
paragraphs: Webhooks have their own section: Settings → Webhooks (group “Connections”, owners only). Owners of a workspace create webhooks there with Create webhook: an address, events and optionally a single database. The list shows each webhook with its format, last delivery and events. Every webhook has a page of its own (/#settings/webhooks/) with the cards Target (format, address, database, credentials for Slack/Matrix), Events (one switch per event), Message (chat formats only), Preview and – for an existing webhook – Delivery with Send test message; Save changes saves it, and it is deleted in the Danger zone with Delete webhook …. The secret key appears once above the list after creating.
Stored credentials (the token for Slack or Matrix) never go to a new address: if you change the address or the format of a webhook with a token, enter the token again, otherwise it isn't saved.

A webhook acts with the rights of the person who created it: it only reports pages, records and comments they may read – content from other people's private spaces stays out, as do hidden properties. If that person is deactivated or leaves the workspace, the webhook stops delivering. Its address and secret are stored encrypted.
Event When
row.created A new record in a database, also from a form
row.updated A record changed (changed names the properties)
row.done A record became done (status "Done" or similar, or the database's done rule)
form.submitted A form answer
page.created A new page
comment.created A new comment on a page or record (text)
mention Someone was mentioned in a page or record (userId, text = the name)
digest.due Once a day at the chosen time: open records due today or overdue (items)
Flowplan sends JSON with POST:
"event": "row.created",
"workspaceId": "…",
"data": { "pageId": "…", "rowId": "…", "cells": { "title": "New" } }
The test message from the settings arrives with the event test.

en.heading: Check the signature
paragraphs: The header X-Flowplan-Signature: sha256= is the HMAC-SHA256 signature of the body with the secret key that is shown once when the webhook is created:
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
const expected = "sha256=" + createHmac("sha256", secret).update(rawBody).digest("hex");
const valid = timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(req.headers["x-flowplan-signature"]));

en.heading: Delivery
paragraphs: – Answers with status 2xx count as delivered; otherwise Flowplan retries up to six times with growing intervals.
– The list under Settings → Webhooks shows each webhook's format, last delivery or last error and its events.
– Only public HTTPS addresses are allowed. For services in the same network (Home Assistant, n8n) the administrators set FLOWPLAN_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=true.

– Send test message in the list or on the webhook's page (card Delivery) sends a sample message right away and shows the result; it is not retried. Below the last delivery the list also shows the last error and when it happened.

en.heading: Create webhooks via the API
paragraphs: With a write token of an owner, webhooks can also be created, changed and removed via the API (POST /api/webhooks, POST /api/webhooks/update, a test message with POST /api/webhooks/test; remove one with POST /api/command and {"action": "webhook.delete", …}), for instance by automation services. Read tokens cannot.

en.heading: Chat notifications
paragraphs: Instead of JSON, a webhook can post a ready message to a chat. On the webhook's page under Settings → Webhooks, choose the format in the card Target:
Format Target What arrives
JSON n8n, Home Assistant, your own services The signed JSON above
Slack Incoming Webhook or a Slack app Block Kit: header, text with the record as a link, fields for changed properties, a line with who and when
Matrix Room webhook (e.g. hookshot) or the Matrix client API HTML message (formatted_body) with plain text as body
Microsoft Teams Incoming Webhook or the workflow "Post to a channel when a webhook request is received" Adaptive Card with a fact list and an Open in Flowplan button
Discord Channel webhook Embed with title, link, fields and timestamp
Next to the form a preview shows the message for a sample event, and below it the content that is actually sent.

en.heading: Setup
paragraphs: Slack
– Messages only: Create an app in Slack (api.slack.com/apps), turn on Incoming Webhooks, pick a channel and enter the address https://hooks.slack.com/services/… in Flowplan.

– With thread replies: Give the app the chat:write scope under OAuth & Permissions, install it and enter the Bot User OAuth Token (xoxb-…) and the channel ID (in Slack: channel details, at the bottom); invite the bot to the channel (/invite @App). For replies, also enter the signing secret (Basic Information). After saving, the webhook's page (card Delivery) shows a Request URL (…/api/webhooks/slack/): turn on Event Subscriptions in the app, enter that address and subscribe to the bot event message.channels (message.groups for private channels). Replies in the thread of a Flowplan message then appear as a comment on the record – written in the name of the person who set up the webhook, prefixed with "Slack:". Threads are matched for 30 days.
Matrix
– Room webhook: Create a "generic webhook" in the room with a bridge such as hookshot and enter its address. Flowplan sends text and html (plus the fields of a Matrix message).

– Client API: Create an access token for a bot account, invite the account to the room and enter the homeserver address (e.g. https://matrix.example.org), the access token and the room (!id:server or #alias:server) in Flowplan. Flowplan sends with PUT /_matrix/client/v3/rooms/{room}/send/m.room.message/{txn}; retries of the same delivery never create duplicate messages.
Microsoft Teams
– In Teams, add a workflow to the channel from the template "Post to a channel when a webhook request is received" (or a classic Incoming Webhook) and enter the address it shows.
Discord
– In the channel settings under Integrations → Webhooks create a webhook and enter the address https://discord.com/api/webhooks/…. Mentions (@everyone etc.) are never triggered.

Access tokens, bot tokens and signing secrets are stored encrypted and never shown again; when editing, an empty field keeps the stored value, and Remove stored credentials deletes them. Chat addresses follow the same rule as other webhooks: public HTTPS only, and every delivery checks the address again.

en.heading: Templates
paragraphs: Every event has a default text that you can change in the form (Template for event). The buttons insert placeholders:
Placeholder Content
{title} Title of the record or page
{actor} Who caused it
{page} Database or parent page
{changes} Changed properties as a list (in the digest: the due records)
{url} Link in Flowplan
{text} Comment text or the name of the mentioned person
{date} Date and time (in the digest: the day)
{count} Number of changes or due records

A small Markdown is allowed: bold, _italic_, ` code , text, lines starting with - as a list and > as a quote. Flowplan converts it to the platform's markup (Slack mrkdwn, Matrix HTML, Teams Markdown, Discord Markdown). Values from Flowplan are never read as markup – a in a title stays a . When {changes}` is not in the template, Slack, Teams and Discord show the changes as fields of their own and Matrix as a list below. Long values are shortened (titles 200 characters, comments 1,000, at most 10 changes and 25 due records) so the platforms' limits are kept. The language of the messages (default texts, date format) is set per webhook.
Example:
{actor} changed [{title}]({url}) in **{page}**:
{changes}

en.heading: Daily digest
paragraphs: With the event Due today (digest.due, "daily at …") a list of the open records that are due today or overdue arrives once a day at the chosen time (the browser's time zone when the webhook was created) – from all databases of the workspace or only the chosen one. The due date is the date property with "Due", "Fällig", "Deadline" or similar in its name, otherwise the first date property; done is what the database's done rule says. Private records are never listed. When nothing is due, nothing is sent.

en.heading: Inbound e-mail
paragraphs: Workspace owners create addresses with Create address under Settings → General → Inbound e-mail that file incoming e-mail in Flowplan:

– Target page: every e-mail becomes a new subpage. The subject is the title, the text (cleaned HTML or plain text) the content, with sender and date above it. Attachments become files of the new page; embedded images (cid:) appear in place, all other attachments as a list below.

– Target database: every e-mail becomes a record. The subject is the title, the text the record's content, the sender address goes into the first e-mail property (if there is one), the e-mail's date is the creation date, and attachments go into the first files property (otherwise as a list into the content).
– Allowed senders: addresses (ada@example.org) or domains (example.org, exactly that domain). E-mails from other senders are not stored but noted in the audit log.
– Signing key (optional): see below.
The address acts with the permissions of the person who created it. If they lose write access to the target or the target is locked, the address stops accepting mail (the list shows the error).
Security and limits:
– Every address has a random 32-character token. Generate a new token invalidates the current address at once.
– HTML from e-mails is cleaned like guest content: no scripts, forms, styles or frames; remote images (e.g. tracking pixels) are removed, links stay.

– Attachments: at most 20 per e-mail, 10 MB per file, 25 MB together; larger ones are named in the text. The file type is checked against the content, photos lose their location; only images and PDFs open in the browser, everything else is downloaded. Attachments count towards the workspace's storage quota and the daily budget for anonymous uploads (200 MB per address and day, plus FLOWPLAN_ANONYMOUS_UPLOAD_MB for the whole instance).
– At most 60 e-mails per address and hour (rejected ones count too); beyond that Flowplan answers 429 and the provider retries later.
– The same Message-ID is stored only once per address. Without a Message-ID, sender, subject, date and text count.
– The sender address of an e-mail can be forged. The sender list is a pre-filter; above all the token must stay secret. For webhooks the signing key adds protection.

en.heading: Via webhook (Mailgun, Postmark, SendGrid, Cloudflare)
paragraphs: Without further setup Flowplan accepts e-mail as a POST to the webhook address shown in the list:
https://flowplan.example.com/api/inbound-mail/<token>
Flowplan recognises the format from the content:
Provider Setup

Mailgun Receiving → Create Route: an expression such as match_recipient("flowplan@mg.example.com"), action Forward to the webhook address. Enter Mailgun's HTTP webhook signing key as the signing key; Flowplan then checks timestamp, token and signature (at most 15 minutes old).
Postmark Server → Inbound stream → Webhook URL = the webhook address. Postmark sends JSON with FromFull, TextBody, HtmlBody and Attachments.

SendGrid Settings → Inbound Parse → Add Host & URL: domain and webhook address. With POST the raw, full MIME message the whole e-mail arrives (email), otherwise the fields from, subject, text, html, attachment-info and attachment1….
Cloudflare Email Routing An Email Worker rule that passes on the raw e-mail (example below).

Your own scripts JSON or multipart/form-data with from, to, subject, text, html, messageId, date and attachments (JSON: [{ "filename", "contentType", "content" (base64), "contentId" }], multipart: file fields) – or the whole e-mail as raw (text) or rawBase64, or as the body with Content-Type: message/rfc822.
Cloudflare Email Worker:
export default {
async email(message, env) {
const raw = await new Response(message.raw).arrayBuffer();
const body = new Uint8Array(raw);
const key = await crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", new TextEncoder().encode(env.FLOWPLAN_KEY), { name: "HMAC", hash: "SHA-256" }, false, ["sign"]);
const sig = [...new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.sign("HMAC", key, body))].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join("");
const res = await fetch(env.FLOWPLAN_URL, {
method: "POST",
headers: { "Content-Type": "message/rfc822", "X-Flowplan-Signature": `sha256=${sig}` },
body,
if (!res.ok) message.setReject(`Flowplan: ${res.status}`);

Signing key: when an address has one, every delivery needs either the header X-Flowplan-Signature: sha256= (HMAC-SHA256 of the unchanged body with the key, as with Flowplan's own webhooks) or Mailgun's signature fields. Otherwise Flowplan answers 401.

Answers: 200 with {"status": "stored" "duplicate" "rejected"} – rejected and duplicate e-mails get 200 too, so the provider does not retry. 401 invalid signature, 404 unknown token, 409 target not writable, 413 too large or daily budget reached, 415 unknown format, 429 hourly limit.

en.heading: Via an IMAP mailbox
paragraphs: Instead of a provider, Flowplan can poll a mailbox of your own (every two minutes, unread e-mail). The administrators set INBOUND_IMAP_HOST, INBOUND_IMAP_USER, INBOUND_IMAP_PASSWORD and INBOUND_MAIL_DOMAIN for it (Configuration). Each address in the list then reads
inbox+<token>@mail.example.com

(plus addressing: the part before + is the mailbox's user name). Flowplan looks for the token in To, Cc, Delivered-To and X-Original-To. Processed, duplicate, rejected and unroutable e-mails are marked as read; when the hourly limit or daily budget is reached they stay unread for the next round.

en.heading: Via the API
paragraphs: With an owner's write token: GET /api/inbound-mail?workspace= lists the addresses; POST /api/command with inbound.save (create or change: pageId, senders, optionally label, secret, id), inbound.rotate and inbound.delete manages them.

en.heading: OpenAPI and SDKs
paragraphs: Every instance describes its own API as an OpenAPI 3.1 document:
– GET /api/openapi.json – the document. Its servers entry carries the instance's address (APP_URL).
– /api/docs – the same description for reading: every path by section, parameters, requests, answers and schemas.

Both are only available to signed-in people and with an API token (Authorization: Bearer fp_…, any scope); without signing in /api/openapi.json answers 401 and /api/docs asks to sign in. Instances that want to show the description publicly set FLOWPLAN_PUBLIC_API_DOCS=true; visitors then only see the major version (0.x) under info.version, signed-in people the exact one.
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer fp_…" https://flowplan.example.com/api/openapi.json > openapi.json

It lists every endpoint an API token may call: workspace and pages, search, files, imports and exports, webhooks, the MCP server and POST /api/command with a schema for each commonly used action (page.create, row.create, row.update, webhook.delete …) plus the list of all other actions. Each endpoint names its error codes (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 413, 429) and the rate limits; calendar subscriptions and CalDAV are noted as external accesses with their own link.

Uploaded images have a placeholder: the answer of POST /api/upload names, under placeholder, the size the image is shown in (w, h) and a ThumbHash (hash, base64) – a blurred preview in about 25 bytes. GET /api/files/placeholders?ids=… returns the same for up to 100 files and profile pictures (avatar:), but only for files you may download; anything else is left out of the answer. For older files the placeholder is computed on the first request. Files of encrypted spaces never have one – the server cannot see their content.

The document is built from the code: where the server validates input with zod (properties and views of a database, the actions, export options), the same schemas are used; the rest is described from the routes in lib/openapi.ts. A test keeps them together – every route under app/api, every action of command() and the SDKs.

en.heading: Clients
paragraphs: Two thin, dependency-free clients are generated from the document, in the source under sdk/:
– TypeScript (sdk/typescript/flowplan.ts): one file, ESM, built on fetch, with types for every answer and action. Copy the file into your project and you are done:
import { FlowplanClient } from "./flowplan.js";
const client = new FlowplanClient({ baseUrl: "https://flowplan.example.com", token: "fp_…" });
const { workspace, pages } = await client.bootstrap();
const { id } = await client.command({ action: "row.create", pageId: "<database ID>", cells: { title: "From the SDK" } });
– Python (sdk/python/flowplan_client.py): standard library only (urllib), Python 3.11 or newer, TypedDicts for the answers:
from flowplan_client import FlowplanClient
client = FlowplanClient("https://flowplan.example.com", token="fp_…")
shell = client.bootstrap()
created = client.command({"action": "row.create", "pageId": "<database ID>", "cells": {"title": "From the SDK"}})

Methods are named after the document's operationId (getPage / get_page, search, uploadFile / upload_file, markdownExport / markdown_export …). Answers outside 2xx raise FlowplanError with the status, the server's message and, for 429, the time to wait. Each SDK comes with a README and an example script.

Both clients send an Idempotency-Key with every change on their own and retry by themselves – GET requests and changes after a network error, 429, 502, 503, 504 or 409 while the first attempt still runs, twice by default (retries, 0 turns it off). Changes are retried with the same key and so applied once. To repeat an action later, pass your own key: idempotencyKey (TypeScript, in the options of a call) or idempotency_key= (Python).
If you build Flowplan yourself, npm run sdk regenerates the clients; the test tests/openapi.test.ts fails when the committed files no longer match the document.

en.heading: Tags and properties via the API
paragraphs: – GET /api/tags?workspace= – the workspace's tags (id, name, color, position, pages, records: number of readable database records with the tag) and properties (id, name, type, options). GET /api/tags/?workspace= also returns the readable pages (pages) and records (records: page_id, row_id, title, database, space_id, updated_at, tags) with that tag.
– GET /api/pages/ contains properties: tags (tag IDs), values (by property ID) and info (created/changed at/by).

– POST /api/command with page.properties: { "action": "page.properties", "pageId": "…", "addTags": ["Customer"], "values": { "Status": "Open", "Budget": 1200 } }. Tags and properties go by ID or name; tags replaces all tags, addTags/removeTags change them, null removes a value.

– POST /api/command with page.collapseProperties: { "action": "page.collapseProperties", "pageId": "…", "collapsed": true } collapses the bar with tags and properties for you (false expands, null back to the default). Applies only to you, on all devices; read access to the page is enough.
– pages.tag adds or removes tags on up to 500 pages at once.

– Owners (for a space's tags and properties also that space's owners): tag.save, tag.delete, tag.merge, tag.reorder, property.save, property.delete, property.reorder. New tags (tag.save without tagId) with spaceId may also be created by members who may write in that space; without spaceId (or null) a new tag or property applies to the whole workspace (owners only).

– Scopes (more): tags and properties in GET /api/tags carry spaceId (null: the whole workspace); GET /api/tags/?sameName=1 adds same-named tags of other spaces. tag.scope/property.scope ({ workspaceId, tagId propertyId, spaceId, resolve?: "block" "copy" "remove", mergeSameName? }, owners only) change the scope, meta.usage ({ workspaceId, kind, id, spaceId }) shows the use outside the target first.

– Moving: page.moveCheck (like page.move) lists the tags and properties of the current space the destination lacks (foreign, with sameName and candidates). page.move and pages.bulk take the choice as meta: { "tags": { "": { "action": "map", "to": "" } }, "properties": { "": { "action": "copy" } } } or short "auto" (map to the same-named ones, else copy), "copy", "remove". Without a choice, page.move answers 409 instead of dropping values.

– Templates: template.save without spaceId belongs to the page's space, with spaceId: null to the whole workspace (owners; a space's tags: 409 or spaceMeta: "remove"). template.dependencies ({ workspaceId, templateId, spaceId }) lists what a template of another space brings (keys tag:, property:); page.create, template.apply and template.copy ({ workspaceId, templateId, spaceId, meta? }) take the choice as meta, template.update changes a template's scope with spaceId. GET /api/templates returns space_id and space_name.

– Text properties (except the title) hold inline Markdown – in row.create, row.update, rows.bulk, rows.import, when reading and in webhooks: bold, _italic_, ~~strikethrough~~, ` code , label (http, https, mailto only), \n for a line break. Send plain text escaped: a backslash before \ * _ ~ [ ] ``. See Formatted text.

– Database properties with the tags as options: in database.update a multiselect property with "tagOptions": true (the server sets its options). Cells hold tag names; a new name in row.create, row.update or rows.bulk creates the tag (members with edit rights, 403 otherwise); rows.import leaves out names that may not become tags. MCP lists such properties in get_database with tagOptions: true.

– In GET /api/search, #tag, -#tag, name:value, OR, NOT, parentheses, created_by:, created:, type:, in: and title: act as filters (parameter tz: the time zone for today and similar) (see Search). MCP clients get tags and values with read_page as frontmatter.

en.heading: Record versions
paragraphs: row.update carries the version of the record you read. If the record changed since, the server answers 409 – unless you also send base: the values of the changed properties as you read them. Then the change applies as long as nobody else changed those properties meanwhile, and only a real conflict (someone changed the same property) gets the 409. Answers to row.update and the other changes of a record (row.move, row.schedule …) include its new rowVersion; send that with the next change.

en.heading: Collections via the API
paragraphs: – GET /api/collections?workspace= – your collections and those shared with the workspace, in your order: id, name, icon, query, shared, mine, canEdit, ownerName.

– GET /api/collections/?tz=Europe/Berlin – runs a collection. It returns collection, items (pageId, rowId, type, title, icon, spaceId, database, tags, createdAt, updatedAt, createdBy, creatorName; most recently changed first, at most 500), total, truncated and encryptedLeftOut. Matches always follow the permissions of the token's person.
– GET /api/collections/preview?workspace=&q= – the first 50 matches of a query that is not saved, and its canonical form (query).
– POST /api/command:
– collection.create { workspaceId, name, query, icon?, shared? }
– collection.update { collectionId, name?, query?, icon?, shared? }
– collection.delete / collection.restore { collectionId }
– collection.duplicate { collectionId, name? }
– collection.reorder { workspaceId, order: [ids] } The query is stored in its canonical form and returned as query. search.save and search.delete still work and create or delete collections.
– MCP: list_collections, run_collection (read), save_collection, delete_collection (write).

en.heading: Workflows
paragraphs: Workflows can be driven entirely through the API (all routes in the OpenAPI document under Workflows):
Route Purpose
GET /api/workflows?workspaceId= List with status, “runs as” and last run
GET /api/workflows/catalog Node catalogue with settings as JSON Schema
GET /api/workflows/{id} Status, active version, draft with its check (editors)
POST /api/workflows/{id}/draft Replace the draft by a graph JSON
POST /api/workflows/{id}/test Dry run or test run of the draft
POST /api/workflows/{id}/activate Activate – you become the person it runs as (write token)
POST /api/workflows/{id}/pause Pause, optionally cancel open runs
POST /api/workflows/{id}/run Start a workflow with a manual trigger
GET /api/workflows/{id}/runs, GET /api/workflow-runs/{runId} Runs and steps
POST /api/workflow-runs/{runId}/retry / cancel Retry from the failed node / cancel
GET /api/workflows/{id}/export, POST /api/workflows/import JSON export (without secrets) and import as a draft

Read tokens only read. Approvals are decided only by a signed-in person, never by a token. activate, run and import take an Idempotency-Key. The SDKs have methods for all of it (saveWorkflowDraft, testWorkflow, activateWorkflow, runWorkflow …).

en.heading: Inbound workflow webhook
paragraphs: The Inbound webhook trigger has an address of its own, POST /api/workflow-hooks/ (shown in the node, can be rotated). The default is signed: X-Flowplan-Timestamp (Unix seconds, at most 5 minutes old) and X-Flowplan-Signature: sha256=. Each signature counts once. The answer is 202 right away, with the run's ID.
body='{"title":"Server down","description":"web-1 is not answering"}'
ts=$(date +%s)
sig=$(printf '%s.%s' "$ts" "$body" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" | cut -d' ' -f2)
curl -X POST "$URL" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Flowplan-Timestamp: $ts" -H "X-Flowplan-Signature: sha256=$sig" -d "$body"
const ts = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000).toString();
const sig = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${ts}.${body}`).digest("hex");
await fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "X-Flowplan-Timestamp": ts, "X-Flowplan-Signature": `sha256=${sig}` }, body });
ts = str(int(time.time()))
sig = hmac.new(secret.encode(), f"{ts}.{body}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, body.encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json", "X-Flowplan-Timestamp": ts, "X-Flowplan-Signature": "sha256=" + sig}))

For services that cannot sign there is the deliberately chosen Token only mode (at most 10 calls a minute). A workflow's HTTP node sends an outgoing Idempotency-Key: ::, so retries do not act twice at the receiver.

en.heading: n8n
paragraphs: For n8n there is the community node n8n-nodes-flowplan (source under integrations/n8n).
– In n8n, install n8n-nodes-flowplan under Settings → Community Nodes.
– Add a Flowplan API credential: your instance address and an API token.
– Use the nodes:
– Flowplan lists workspaces and pages, creates pages (optionally with Markdown content), reads, creates and updates database records (properties by name) and searches.

– Flowplan Trigger starts workflows on new or changed records, form answers and new pages. It registers its own webhook on activation (which needs a write token of an owner), removes it on deactivation and rejects deliveries with a wrong signature.
If n8n runs in your own network, set FLOWPLAN_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=true (Configuration).

en.heading: Calendar subscriptions
paragraphs: Calendar views can be subscribed to as an iCalendar link, see Views.
With the browser extension you save web pages to Flowplan in one click: the whole article, just the selection, a bookmark or single highlights. It runs in Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera and Firefox.

en.heading: Setting up
paragraphs: – In Flowplan, create a personal API token under Settings → API & AI assistants (or Settings → Web clipper → Create token) and choose the permission Browser extension only. Such a token can do nothing else: it opens neither the API nor MCP and cannot read anything but the list of your targets.
– Install the extension (see below) and click its icon.
– Enter the address of your instance, for example https://flowplan.example.com, and the token. The browser now asks once for access to exactly this address – the extension never accesses other sites.
Sign out in the extension's window removes the token from the browser and gives up the access to the instance. You can revoke the token in the settings at any time.

en.heading: Saving
paragraphs: Click the extension's icon or press Alt+Shift+F. Choose the target – the extension remembers it – and optionally tags:

– Whole page: the extension finds the actual article and leaves out navigation, ads, cookie notices, comments and sidebars. Links and images keep pointing to the original page. The link to the source sits at the top of the new page.
– Selection: only the selected part of the page, with formatting and links.
– Bookmark only: title, address, description and favicon go into the space's Lesezeichen (bookmarks) database (see Web clipper). Duplicate links are refused.
Depending on the target you get:
Target Whole page / selection Bookmark
A space a new page in the space a record in its bookmarks database
A page a new sub-page a record in the bookmarks database of its space
A database a new record with the text as its document; the link goes into the first URL property as for a page

Tags go into a property named Tags (or Schlagwörter, Labels) when the database has one; new tags are added as options. In the bookmarks database the extension creates the Tags property the first time. On pages the tags appear as #tag below the source link.
The server cleans the content once more: scripts, forms, embedded foreign pages and event attributes are dropped, just like when pasting into the editor.

en.heading: Highlights
paragraphs: Select text on a web page and choose Highlight in Flowplan in the context menu (or press Alt+Shift+H). The passage is appended as a quote with a link to the source:
– If the target is a page, all highlights end up one below the other on that page.
– If the target is a space, the first highlight of a web page creates a new page for that source; further highlights of the same web page go onto the same page.
– If the target is a database, every highlight becomes a record.
A green check mark on the icon confirms the save, a red exclamation mark reports an error (such as an expired token).
Change the shortcuts in Chrome at chrome://extensions/shortcuts, in Firefox under Add-ons → gear → Manage Extension Shortcuts.

en.heading: Installing
paragraphs: The extension lives in the source code under extensions/browser/ and needs no build step.
– Chrome, Edge, Brave: open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, click Load unpacked and choose the folder extensions/browser.
– Firefox: open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox and Load Temporary Add-on → extensions/browser/manifest.json. For a permanent installation, have the ZIP signed at addons.mozilla.org.
– Building the package: npm run extension:zip writes extensions/browser/dist/flowplan-.zip – upload this file to the Chrome Web Store, Edge Add-ons or addons.mozilla.org.

en.heading: Privacy and permissions
paragraphs: – The extension reads a page only when you call it (icon, context menu or shortcut) – it does not run in the background on every page.

– Permissions: activeTab (the current page, only after your click), scripting (to read it then), contextMenus, storage (address, token, the target chosen last) and access to exactly your Flowplan address, asked for only when connecting.
– It only sends to your instance. Cookies are not sent along; the token alone signs in.
– End-to-end encrypted spaces are not offered as targets: the server never writes plaintext into them.
– The server allows requests from browser extensions (CORS) only for the two clipper addresses /api/clipper/targets and /api/clipper/save, and only with a token – see API and webhooks.

In cluster mode, several Flowplan instances serve one installation: one PostgreSQL database, one Redis, one S3 bucket and any number of instances behind a load balancer – for more people active at the same time and updates without downtime.

en.heading: Do you need it?
paragraphs: Most teams do not: a single container carries about 20 simultaneously active people with SQLite and about 30 with PostgreSQL (see Sizing). Cluster mode pays off when more people regularly work at the same time, or when Flowplan should keep running through updates and the loss of a server. In return it brings three services you have to run (or rent) and back up.

en.heading: Requirements
paragraphs: Switch it on with FLOWPLAN_CLUSTER=1. Then these are required:
What Variable For
PostgreSQL 16+ DATABASE_URL=postgres://… All data. SQLite is a file on one host and does not work. See PostgreSQL.
Redis (tested with 7) REDIS_URL=redis://… or rediss://… (TLS) Live editing, presence and rate limits between the instances. Redis does not need to persist any of it.
S3 storage S3_BUCKET, S3_ENDPOINT, S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID, S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY All files; the local uploads/ folder is only a cache. See Storage, S3 and backups.
If one is missing, an instance does not start and lists every problem at once in the log. REDIS_URL without cluster mode is ignored with a warning.

Also required – here too an instance refuses to start without them: keys that are identical on every instance. A single container creates some keys itself in its data folder – in a cluster every instance has its own folder, and each would create different ones. So set the same values everywhere:

– FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY or FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY (or their …_FILE variants, e.g. for Docker secrets) – otherwise an instance cannot read stored secrets and signatures of the others (two-factor sign-in, AI keys, unlocked share links). See Stored secrets.
– WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY and WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY (a VAPID key pair, e.g. from npx web-push generate-vapid-keys) – otherwise push subscriptions only match one instance. See Push notifications.

Coming from a single container without these variables, take the values from its data folder so stored secrets and push subscriptions stay valid: the content of secrets.key as FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY (in addition to a FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY; both are read), and publicKey/privateKey from web-push-keys.json as WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY/WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY.

en.heading: What the instances share
paragraphs: – Live editing and presence: changes to documents, records and whiteboards, cursors and "who is here" reach every instance through Redis. Two people on different instances work together as on one. The data itself is in PostgreSQL; if a message is lost, the browser catches up on its next sync. No sticky sessions are needed.
– Rate limits: limits such as those for AI requests count across all instances (through Redis). Limits already kept in the database (failed sign-ins, demos, MCP) applied to all of them anyway.

– Leader-only jobs: exactly one instance leads at any time (elected through a lock in PostgreSQL). Only it runs the timed jobs: reminders, automations, page reviews, the search indexer, text extraction from files, cleanup and retention, digests, scheduled backups and Markdown exports, LDAP, calendar and issue sync, inbound e-mail, Telegram, AI background work and the monitoring alerts. If it fails, another one takes over within seconds.
– Queues: every instance sends e-mails, push messages, webhooks and chat-app messages; each message is taken by exactly one instance.

– Files: an uploaded file first lands in the cache of the instance that received it, which uploads it to the bucket right away (usually well under a second). Other instances fetch it from the bucket when needed and wait up to 5 seconds for it.

en.heading: Health, readiness and shutdown
paragraphs: Address Answers Meant for
/api/health/live 200 as long as the process answers – no database check, since a restart does not fix a database outage Liveness probe
/api/health/ready 200 when the database, Redis and the bucket answer; 503 otherwise and while shutting down Readiness probe, load balancer
/api/health as before, see Health check Docker health check, apps
Without a token, /api/health/ready only answers ok/error per check; with FLOWPLAN_METRICS_TOKEN as a bearer token, response times and error messages are added.

FLOWPLAN_READY_REQUIRE decides which checks count for readiness – a list of database, redis and objectStorage, by default all three. The database always counts. If Redis fails, the default turns every instance "not ready" at once and the load balancer has nothing left. With FLOWPLAN_READY_REQUIRE=database,objectStorage they stay ready: editing and saving keep working, only live changes between instances arrive on the next sync, and each instance counts rate limits on its own.

Shutdown: on SIGTERM the instance immediately answers 503 on /api/health/ready, closes its live connections (browsers reconnect through the load balancer to another instance), finishes open requests, hands over the lead and signs off from the others. Give it 30 seconds for this (stop_grace_period, terminationGracePeriodSeconds).

en.heading: Schema before the start
paragraphs: Each instance brings the database schema up to its version on start (under a lock; they wait for each other). Cleaner is a separate step before the instances start, which fails loudly:
DATABASE_URL=postgres://… node /app/scripts/db-schema.mjs

Then set FLOWPLAN_PG_SCHEMA_AUTO=off for the instances. The Docker Compose example and the Helm chart work this way. The schema is only extended, never shrunk: during a rolling update, old and new instances run side by side.

en.heading: Docker Compose
paragraphs: A complete example lives in deploy/compose/cluster: PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7 with a password and without persistence, MinIO as S3 including bucket creation, the schema step, two Flowplan instances and Caddy as load balancer. It is meant for trying things out on one host and as a starting point; in production, run the database, Redis and storage as separate, backed-up services.
git clone https://github.com/yannicschuller/flowplan.git
cd flowplan/deploy/compose/cluster
cp .env.example .env    # replace every "change-me" value
docker compose up -d
In it:

– .env holds APP_URL, FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN and the passwords for PostgreSQL (POSTGRES_PASSWORD and POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD), Redis and MinIO – placeholders only, to be replaced. FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY and WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY are required too – empty in .env.example; without them docker compose up stops with a hint (see Requirements).
– The schema service runs once before the instances (node /app/scripts/db-schema.mjs); the instances have FLOWPLAN_PG_SCHEMA_AUTO=off.

– flowplan-1 and flowplan-2 each have their own volume as a cache, FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL=20 and a health check on /api/health/ready. More instances: copy the flowplan-2 service and add it to the Caddyfile.

– Caddy distributes round robin over ready instances (health check on /api/health/ready) and passes live connections through unbuffered (flush_interval -1). For HTTPS, replace :8080 in the Caddyfile with your host name.

– PostgreSQL runs with max_connections=200. Flowplan connects as the role flowplan, which owns the database but is no superuser: POSTGRES_PASSWORD is its password, POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD that of the image's superuser postgres, for administration only. On the database's first start postgres-init.sh creates the role and installs pg_trgm (and pgvector when the image has it) into flowplan_ext. A volume made with an older version of the example keeps its roles – there flowplan is still a superuser until you demote it.

Another load balancer (nginx, Traefik, HAProxy) needs the same: health check on /api/health/ready, no buffering for server-sent events (/api/documents/live and the cursor channels), long read timeouts, uploads up to 110 MB and FLOWPLAN_TRUSTED_PROXIES matching the number of proxies.

en.heading: Kubernetes (Helm)
paragraphs: The chart in deploy/helm/flowplan has cluster mode built in (cluster.enabled=true). It does not create PostgreSQL, Redis or S3 – use managed services or their own charts. The connection addresses live only in Secrets you create yourself:
kubectl create namespace flowplan
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-cluster \
--from-literal=DATABASE_URL='postgres://flowplan:<password>@postgres:5432/flowplan' \
--from-literal=REDIS_URL='redis://:<password>@redis-master:6379/0'
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-env \
--from-literal=S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<key-id>' \
--from-literal=S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='<secret>'
# the keys every pod shares (push keys: npx web-push generate-vapid-keys)
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-keys \
--from-literal=FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
--from-literal=WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY='<public VAPID key>' \
--from-literal=WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY='<private VAPID key>'
helm install flowplan deploy/helm/flowplan -n flowplan \
--set appUrl=https://flowplan.example.org \
--set existingSecret=flowplan-env \
--set cluster.enabled=true \
--set cluster.replicas=3 \
--set cluster.database.existingSecret=flowplan-cluster \
--set cluster.redis.existingSecret=flowplan-cluster \
--set cluster.keys.existingSecret=flowplan-keys \
--set s3.bucket=flowplan --set s3.endpoint=https://s3.example.org
What the chart does in cluster mode:
– Schema job as a pre-install/pre-upgrade hook (node /app/scripts/db-schema.mjs) before pods of a new version start. Without it (cluster.migration.enabled=false) the pods do it on start.
– Rolling updates without downtime (maxUnavailable: 0), a PodDisruptionBudget (cluster.podDisruptionBudget.minAvailable, default 1) and pods spread over nodes where possible.
– Probes: liveness on /api/health/live, readiness on /api/health/ready; before stopping, a pod waits cluster.preStopSeconds (5) so the load balancer takes it out.
– No volume: /app/data is an emptyDir per pod (cluster.cacheSizeLimit, 5 Gi); files live in the bucket, backups come from PostgreSQL (pg_dump).

– Database role: the role in DATABASE_URL should own the database but not be a superuser. Many PostgreSQL charts make their user a superuser – create a role of its own then, see Role without superuser rights.
– Connections: cluster.poolSize (10) per pod plus two of its own; replicas × (poolSize + 2) must stay below the server's max_connections.

– Shared keys: every pod gets FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY and WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY from the Secret in cluster.keys.existingSecret. If the keys are named differently in your Secret, name them with cluster.keys.encryptionKey, cluster.keys.webPushPublicKey and cluster.keys.webPushPrivateKey. Keep a copy of the encryption key apart from the backups.
– The chart refuses to install if the database, Redis, the bucket or cluster.keys.existingSecret is missing.

With ingress-nginx, set the annotations nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off" and nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600" for live connections, and nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: 110m for uploads. The chart's README explains every value.

en.heading: Administration → Monitoring → System
paragraphs: The System section under Administration → Monitoring shows how the installation runs:
– Mode (single container, or cluster with the number of instances), Database with version and reachability,
– Connections of this instance (open, idle, waiting) and the Timeouts,
– Redis with version and messages sent, received and failed, Object storage with bucket and reachability,
– the Leader and since when it leads,
– the Shared queues (files, mail, push, webhooks, chat apps),
– in a cluster, a table of all Instances with their state (leader, ready, stopping), busy and waiting connections, memory and last heartbeat. An instance silent for 30 seconds drops off the list.
"Waiting" connections mean requests are waiting for a free database connection – raise FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL or add instances.

en.heading: More variables
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning
FLOWPLAN_CLUSTER empty 1 (or true, on) switches cluster mode on. Equivalent: FLOWPLAN_MODE=cluster.
REDIS_URL empty redis://:@host:6379/0, with TLS rediss://…. User, password and database number go into the address.
FLOWPLAN_READY_REQUIRE database,redis,objectStorage Checks that decide /api/health/ready (above).
FLOWPLAN_INSTANCE_ID host name + random Name of the instance in the overview and in the application_name of its database connections. The Helm chart uses the pod name.
FLOWPLAN_REDIS_PREFIX flowplan: Prefix for keys and channels when several installations share one Redis.
FLOWPLAN_LEADER_INTERVAL 5000 How often (ms) instances check the lead; decides how fast a failed leader is replaced.

en.heading: Workflows in a cluster
paragraphs: The steps of workflows wait in a queue in the database. Every instance claims steps that are due with a lease (2 minutes); a fencing token makes sure an instance whose lease has run out can no longer commit. If an instance fails, another takes over its steps once the lease has expired. New steps wake the other instances through Redis; without the bus they check on a timer. Schedules and date triggers run only on the leader and exactly once per slot. FLOWPLAN_WORKFLOW_WORKERS sets how many steps an instance runs at once.

en.heading: Known limits
paragraphs: – Files are uploaded by the instance that received them. Until then – normally well under a second – other instances wait up to 5 seconds. A few paths read the local folder directly (exports and archives, some importers, copies when publishing) and can still miss a file just uploaded on another instance. If an instance fails before uploading, the file is lost.

– Restores and instance moves with one instance. An uploaded backup sits in the cache of the instance that received it and is only applied once that instance leads. Applying it replaces every table in one transaction; requests from other instances wait meanwhile and fail after FLOWPLAN_PG_LOCK_TIMEOUT. On Kubernetes, an emptyDir is lost on restart. So scale down to one instance first (cluster.replicas=1, or only flowplan-1), restore, then scale up again. The same goes for the move tool.

– Redis is a single point: if it fails, editing and saving keep working, but live changes between instances only arrive on the next sync, each instance counts rate limits on its own, and with the default FLOWPLAN_READY_REQUIRE every instance turns "not ready" (above).
– No Redis Sentinel and no Redis Cluster: Flowplan talks to exactly one Redis address. A managed Redis with a stable address works.
– Per instance remain the progress displays of restores and moves and the search indexer's backlog figures.

en.heading: Next
paragraphs: – Sizing: how many instances and what hardware.

– Switching the database: bring an existing instance to PostgreSQL. For a cluster, first turn on S3 in the single container and wait until every file is in the bucket (Administration → Storage & backup, or objectStorage.pending at 0 in /api/health).
Several people write on the same page at the same time without overwriting each other. Comments, mentions and the inbox keep conversations next to the content.

en.heading: Edit at the same time
paragraphs: – Documents and record contents are merged with Yjs (CRDT): every change is kept, even when two people type in the same paragraph.

– Changes reach the others within a fraction of a second: the server pushes every saved change right away to everyone who has the same document open (server-sent events). Only what changed is sent, not the whole document.
– Coloured cursors and selections with names show where others are writing; their movements arrive immediately too.
– Without a connection you keep working; changes are merged as soon as the network is back.
– Database changes are checked for version conflicts: if someone changed the same record in the meantime, your change is not silently written over it but refused, and you see the new state.
– Guests with an edit link also work live and see the members' cursors; members see the guests as "Guest · ".
– Whiteboards also have live cursors as in Miro.

en.heading: Suggest changes
paragraphs: The pen button Suggest in the toolbar turns on suggestion mode. Typing then does not change the text directly:
– Inserted text appears underlined in green, deleted text stays in place, struck through in red. Typing over a selection creates both.
– Deleting your own suggestion removes it completely.

– Above the text, a bar shows the number of open suggestions. Expanded, it lists each one with person and text; a click jumps to the spot. ✓ accepts a suggestion (the insertion stays, the deleted text disappears), ✗ rejects it. Accept all and Reject all settle everything at once.
– Suggestions are part of the document: they appear for everyone right away and stay saved until someone accepts or rejects them. Everyone who may edit the page can accept and reject.
– Formatting, paragraph breaks and moved blocks are applied directly even in suggestion mode; other people's changes never become your suggestions.

– Changes in code blocks are marked as suggestions too. When accepting or rejecting leaves a paragraph or list item completely empty (a suggested new paragraph rejected, a fully deleted one accepted), it disappears as well.
– Suggestions by the AI: in Ask AI, Suggest as changes puts the answer into the page as suggestions in the same way – with your name and "(AI)".

en.heading: Reactions
paragraphs: – Comments: below every page and record comment, the smiley adds a reaction (👍 ❤️ 🎉 😄 👀 ✅ 🙏 🔥). A click on an existing reaction joins it or takes your own back; the tooltip shows who reacted. Everyone who may see the page can react.

– Paragraphs and headings: selecting text or right-clicking in the text opens the text menu. At the top are the reactions for the paragraph, below them formatting (bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, highlight, code, link), Comment and Copy, in tasks also Due date. The reactions sit as small pills on the block, are saved in the document and appear for everyone right away; a click on your own takes it back. This works for everyone who may edit the page. Shift + right-click brings up the browser's menu.
– Text comments have their own reactions in the thread.

en.heading: Follow pages
paragraphs: The bell at the top of a page turns Follow on or off. Whoever follows a page gets a notification as soon as someone else changes it – one per page, until you have looked at it again – and for every new comment on it (for a database: also on its records). With e-mail set up, it lands in the e-mail digest. Whoever creates a page follows it automatically. Under Settings → Notifications, the kind "Changes to pages you follow" can be switched off for inbox, push and e-mail separately.

en.heading: Who has seen the page?
paragraphs: The eye next to the bell shows who opened the page and when. A tick means the person has seen the latest state; "older" means the page has changed since. Only people who may still see the page are shown.

en.heading: Changes since your last visit
paragraphs: If someone else changed a page since you last opened it, a notice with their names appears at the top. For documents, Show changes shows the text changes since your last visit (inserted and deleted, as in the version history). For databases the notice gives the number of edited records.
On the home screen, Recently viewed lists the pages you opened last.

en.heading: Page comments
paragraphs: The speech bubble icon in the header opens the page's comments; comments on database records sit below the record. ⌘ Enter sends. Page and record comments are plain text. @ followed by a member's full name or e-mail address – say @Anna Berg – mentions the person: they get a notification, provided they may see the page and the record.

en.heading: Text comments
paragraphs: Select text and choose Comment on text or press ⌘ ⌥ M.
– The commented text is highlighted; a click on it opens the thread.
– Replies, emoji reactions, Resolve and Reopen.
– Posts can be formatted (lists, links, quotes, code); @ opens the person search.
– Your own posts can be edited and deleted. People newly mentioned in an edit get a notification; those mentioned before are not notified again.
– If the text is deleted later, the quote stays in the thread.
– Drafts stay saved until you send or discard them.
Text comments exist in documents and in the contents of database records, also in exports and content archives.

en.heading: Mentions
paragraphs: – @Name in text or a comment notifies the person. The person search only shows members who may read the page.

– Only people who may see the page – and, for a record, the record – are notified; never the author. Someone who would hear about the comment anyway gets a single notification, the mention. If the page lies in a journal with a PIN, the notification only says “This journal is locked.” until the PIN is entered.
– Guests do not see other members; their mentions notify nobody.

en.heading: Inbox
paragraphs: The Inbox in the sidebar collects mentions, comments and replies that concern you (who hears about comments), date reminders as well as comments and records from guests. Unread items are marked; a click jumps to the spot – for text comments straight into the thread. You choose which events arrive as push notifications under Settings → Notifications (see Search, inbox and push).
All environment variables at a glance. Many values can also be set in the interface of the Administration (see In the interface); values set there take precedence.

en.heading: Required
paragraphs: Variable Example Meaning

APP_URL https://flowplan.example.com The public address exactly as it appears in the browser – scheme, host, port if any, without a trailing slash. The basis for sign-in redirects, cookies, passkeys, links in e-mails and push notifications and the origin check.

en.heading: Sign-in
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning
FLOWPLAN_LOCAL_LOGIN on false turns off e-mail, password and passkeys; then only single sign-on remains.

FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN empty (Helm: generated) Recommended for instances reachable from the internet: the first account and the restore on the setup screen only work via /register?setup=. No effect afterwards. If it is missing and APP_URL is not a local address, Flowplan warns at start in the log and on the setup screen. See Sign-in.
OIDC_ISSUER empty The login provider for single sign-on. Without it there are only e-mail, password and passkeys.
OIDC_CLIENT_ID – Client ID.
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET – Client secret. Never put it into the image or into Git. Empty: a public client, PKCE only.

OIDC_LINKED_SSO_ONLY off true: accounts connected to SSO sign in through SSO only. A password or passkey sign-in is refused with a note; passkeys and the authenticator app stay for confirming important steps. See Connect an existing account to SSO.

OIDC_NEW_ACCOUNTS on false: SSO sign-in creates no new accounts – only existing, connected or SCIM-provisioned accounts sign in. At a first SSO sign-in with a known address, "Create a separate account instead" is then not offered.

SESSION_HOURS 8 Browser session without "Stay signed in": ends this many hours after signing in (1–24). Also under Administration → Sign-in & SSO → Sessions; a value saved there takes precedence (for every SESSION_* except SESSION_MAX_DAYS and SESSION_GROUPS_HOURS).
SESSION_REMEMBER off true offers Stay signed in in the browser when signing in – see Sign-in. The apps stay signed in regardless.
SESSION_IDLE_HOURS 168 With "stay signed in" in the browser: the session ends this many hours after it was last used (1–8760).

SESSION_APP_REMEMBER on The desktop and mobile apps stay signed in while they (or their widgets) are used – for sign-ins the app proves (hand-off through the browser, or password with the app's device key; see Sign-in). false: their sessions end like a browser session without "Stay signed in".
SESSION_APP_DAYS 90 An app's session ends after this many days without use (1–365).

SESSION_MAX_DAYS 30 / 365 Sessions that stay signed in end at the latest this many days after signing in (1–365; default 30 in the browser, 365 in the apps; never shorter than the time without use) – with SSO just as with password and passkey.

SESSION_GROUPS_HOURS empty Only when set: SSO sessions with "stay signed in" end after this many hours already, so group changes at the provider take effect with the new sign-in. Without it they follow through SCIM, the LDAP sync or the next sign-in.
LDAP_URL empty Sign-in with an LDAP directory (ldap:// or ldaps://) – see Sign-in with LDAP.
LDAP_BIND_DN / LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD empty Search account for LDAP; without it, anonymous search.
LDAP_BASE_DN – Where LDAP accounts are searched.
LDAP_USER_FILTER (\ (uid={user})(mail={user})) Search filter; {user} is the escaped sign-in name.
LDAP_GROUP_ATTRIBUTE memberOf Groups for SSO mappings and the admin group, synced hourly.
LDAP_TLS_CA empty CA for ldaps:///StartTLS (path or PEM).
LDAP_STARTTLS false ldap:// with StartTLS.
LDAP_TIMEOUT_MS 8000 Time limit per LDAP operation.
LDAP_CONTACTS_BASE_DN LDAP_BASE_DN Base for contacts from LDAP; the OU tree starts here.
LDAP_CONTACTS_FILTER people without computers Which entries count as contacts.
LDAP_CONTACTS_SYNC_MINUTES 60 Sync of contacts from the directory (15–1440 minutes).
LDAP_CONTACTS_ATTRIBUTES – More LDAP attributes contacts databases may map (separated by commas or spaces), on top of those of the default mapping.
LDAP_CONTACTS on off turns contacts from LDAP off.
The other OIDC variables and everything about passwords and passkeys are described under Sign-in.

en.heading: Operations
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning
FLOWPLAN_DATA_DIR /app/data in the image, ./data otherwise Data directory for SQLite, uploads, push keys and text recognition data.

PUID / PGID 1000 / same as PUID Only in the image and only when the container starts as root (user: "0:0"): Flowplan gives the data folder to this user and group and runs as them, never as root. Often simpler: user: "UID:GID" – see Volume permissions.
FLOWPLAN_WORKSPACE_QUOTA_MB unlimited Default storage quota per workspace in MB (0 = unlimited).

FLOWPLAN_IMPORT_MAX_MB empty Largest file for imports from AFFiNE and other tools in MB, for everyone. Without it the largest upload applies (Administration → Limits & retention, or the person's own limit), at least 100 MB. Only the AFFiNE workspace file (.affine) may exceed 100 MB; ZIP exports stay at 100 MB. A proxy in front must let such large requests through.

FLOWPLAN_MAX_DOCUMENT_MB 16 Largest size of a collaboratively edited document (page or record document) in MB. Changes that would make a document grow beyond it are refused ("The document is too large …"); split larger content across several pages. Keeps every edit of a huge document from slowing the server down.

FLOWPLAN_IMPORT_MAX_DOCS 10000 Largest number of pages per import from AFFiNE, Confluence, Evernote, Google Docs, Obsidian and Notion/Markdown: documents, folders, databases, whiteboards and collections; when importing as a new database, the number of records. Above it the preview shows the count and the import is refused (the message names the variable). Documents are converted one at a time; a higher value costs time, hardly memory.

FLOWPLAN_IMPORT_MAX_FILES 20000 Largest number of files (images, attachments) per import from an AFFiNE workspace or snapshot; further ones are left out, the preview names their number and the variable. ZIP exports may have as many entries as pages and files together (at least 12,000).
FLOWPLAN_SNAPSHOT_RETENTION_DAYS 180 How long automatic versions are kept, in days (0 = forever).
FLOWPLAN_OCR on 0 turns off text recognition for scanned PDFs and images.

FLOWPLAN_OCR_LANGS deu,eng Languages of the text recognition, e.g. fra,eng; the first is the main language. deu, eng, fra and chi_sim (Chinese, Simplified, e.g. chi_sim,eng) are bundled. Each extra language costs memory and time per page; Chinese the most (about 100 MB more memory, roughly one and a half times as long per page).

FLOWPLAN_METRICS on off switches off the usage statistics of the monitoring: requests, errors and response times per minute, active people per hour, storage history and AI tokens. Only numbers are collected – no IP addresses, paths or names; minutes are kept 48 hours, hours 35 days, days 400 days. With off nothing is collected, and the switch Collect usage statistics under Administration → Monitoring → Statistics is locked. /api/metrics does not depend on it.
FLOWPLAN_METRICS_TOKEN empty At least 16 characters; enables /api/metrics in Prometheus format. Sent as Authorization: Bearer …, it also unlocks the details of /api/health (see Health check).

FLOWPLAN_PUBLIC_API_DOCS false true makes /api/openapi.json and /api/docs readable without signing in; visitors only see the major version (0.x) there. Otherwise only for signed-in people and API tokens.

FLOWPLAN_UPDATE_CHECK on false turns off the check for new versions (for instances without internet). Otherwise the server asks GitHub for the latest release at most every 12 hours and shows admins a notice in the administration.

FLOWPLAN_UPDATE_URL GitHub API Another address for the latest release (same format as api.github.com/repos/yannicschuller/flowplan/releases/latest), such as an internal mirror. Not to be confused with the desktop app's variable of the same name, which names the app's update source on the computer running it.

FLOWPLAN_TRUSTED_PROXIES 1 Number of proxies in front of Flowplan (Traefik alone: 1, Pangolin in front of Traefik: 2, 0 = trust no header). Decides which entry in X-Forwarded-For is the real address – for limiting sign-in attempts, demo starts and anonymous form answers. Entries made up by the browser are ignored this way. When no address arrives at all (the proxy does not set the header), only the limits per account and per link apply, and the log shows a note once.
FLOWPLAN_SECURITY_LOG on Security events as a JSON line on stdout: on (with address, for fail2ban/CrowdSec), anonymous, off (Security).
FLOWPLAN_SECURITY_RETENTION_DAYS 90 How long security events stay in the database (at least 7).
FLOWPLAN_COUNTRY_HEADER empty The proxy's header with the country of the request (e.g. CF-IPCountry); turns on the rule "two countries in a short time".
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT empty OTLP collector (HTTP); security events go there as OpenTelemetry logs. With OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS and OTEL_SERVICE_NAME.

FLOWPLAN_ANONYMOUS_UPLOAD_MB 1024 How many MB visitors without an account may upload per day on the whole instance – through anonymous forms and editing links (0 = unlimited). Each form or link additionally gets 200 MB per day, independent of the workspace's storage quota.
The Typst preview loads its compiler and fonts (WebAssembly, about 11 MB compressed) on first use from /typst/… of your own server; nothing is fetched from a CDN.

en.heading: S3 and database backup
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning
S3_BUCKET empty Turns S3 on. Without this variable everything stays local.
S3_ENDPOINT AWS API address of the storage, e.g. http://minio:9000.
S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID / S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY – Access keys with read and write access to the bucket.
S3_REGION us-east-1 Region. Garage requires its own value (often garage).
S3_PREFIX flowplan Folder in the bucket; files under /uploads/, the database under /db/.
FLOWPLAN_LITESTREAM on off: only mirror files, do not back up the database.
LITESTREAM_SSE_C_KEY empty Optional: the storage provider encrypts the Litestream replica (SSE-C, 32 bytes base64, only over https and with providers that support SSE-C).
Details: Storage, S3 and backups.

en.heading: Database and cluster
paragraphs: Without these variables, Flowplan uses SQLite in one container. They are also listed, with comments, in the .env.example. Every value with its default and explanation is under PostgreSQL and Cluster mode.
Variable Default Meaning
DATABASE_URL empty postgres://… switches to PostgreSQL. Its role should own the database but not be a superuser (PostgreSQL).
FLOWPLAN_PG_SCHEMA, FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL, FLOWPLAN_PG_*_TIMEOUT public, 10, … Schema, connections per instance and time limits.
FLOWPLAN_PG_PREPARE on off: unnamed queries instead of named prepared statements – for PgBouncer in transaction mode without max_prepared_statements.

DATABASE_SESSION_URL DATABASE_URL A direct connection (or a session-mode pool) for notifications, the lead in a cluster and pg_dump/pg_restore, when DATABASE_URL points at PgBouncer in transaction mode.
FLOWPLAN_BACKUP_FORMAT pg_dump sqlite: scheduled backups on PostgreSQL in the portable SQLite format.
FLOWPLAN_CLUSTER empty 1: several instances; requires DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, S3_BUCKET, FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY (or FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY) and WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY/WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY.
REDIS_URL empty Redis for cluster mode, redis://… or rediss://….
FLOWPLAN_READY_REQUIRE all Which checks decide /api/health/ready.

en.heading: Encryption
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning
FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY empty 32 bytes, base64 (openssl rand -base64 32). Encrypts files in the bucket, scheduled backups, Markdown exports and the instance backup. Without a key nothing changes.
FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE empty Instead of the variable: path to a file holding the key (Docker secret).
FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS empty Earlier keys, comma-separated – only for reading after a key change.
Details: Encryption.

en.heading: Stored secrets
paragraphs: Flowplan stores AI provider keys, the keys of authenticator apps (two-factor sign-in), the access tokens of the Git export of spaces and the tokens of chat apps only encrypted (AES-256-GCM, bound to their place). The key for this comes, in this order, from:
Source Meaning
FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY If set, it also encrypts the stored secrets.
FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY / FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY_FILE A key just for this: 32 bytes, base64 or hex (openssl rand -base64 32), or the path to a file (Docker secret).
secrets.key in the data folder Without the two variables, Flowplan creates this file itself when first needed (readable only by its owner).

[!IMPORTANT] The instance backup deliberately leaves out secrets.key – it doesn't belong next to the data it protects. Back up the file separately or set the key as a variable. If it is missing after a restore, admins and users enter their AI keys and chat-app tokens again, and for two-factor sign-in recovery codes or a reset by an administrator help. The move tool, by contrast, takes secrets.key along, as it moves the whole instance.

en.heading: Instance move
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning

FLOWPLAN_MOVE_ALLOW_PRIVATE empty On the new instance: true allows taking over an instance at an internal address (LAN, VPN, localhost) and over http:// – a home server, say. Without it only public HTTPS addresses. Remove it after the move.
Details: Moving an instance.

en.heading: E-mail (SMTP)
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning
SMTP_HOST empty Turns on sending e-mail: invitations, address confirmations, password resets and digests of unread notifications.
SMTP_PORT 587 Port. With 465 Flowplan speaks TLS directly, STARTTLS otherwise.
SMTP_SECURE by port true/false forces TLS from the start of the connection.
SMTP_USER / SMTP_PASSWORD empty Sign-in at the mail server.
SMTP_FROM Flowplan Sender, e.g. Flowplan .
Check delivery under Administration → E-mail → Send test email.

en.heading: Inbound e-mail (IMAP)
paragraphs: For inbound e-mail via webhook (Mailgun, Postmark, SendGrid, Cloudflare) nothing needs to be set. A mailbox of your own is polled over IMAP every two minutes:
Variable Default Meaning
INBOUND_MAIL_DOMAIN empty Domain of the inbound addresses, e.g. mail.example.com. The settings then show inbox+@mail.example.com for each address.
INBOUND_IMAP_HOST empty Turns on IMAP polling (together with INBOUND_IMAP_USER).
INBOUND_IMAP_PORT 993 Port (143 when INBOUND_IMAP_TLS=false).
INBOUND_IMAP_USER / INBOUND_IMAP_PASSWORD empty Sign-in at the mailbox. The part before @ is also the part before + in the addresses.
INBOUND_IMAP_FOLDER INBOX Folder that is polled.
INBOUND_IMAP_TLS true false only for a mail server on the same host or network (unencrypted).

INBOUND_MAIL_AUTHSERV_ID empty The id (authserv-id) your own receiving mail server or provider starts its Authentication-Results header with, e.g. mx.example.com. Also applies to inbound e-mail via webhook.

The mail server must support plus addressing (inbox+anything@… is delivered to inbox@…); Dovecot, Postfix, Gmail/Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 (switch it on there) do. Flowplan marks processed e-mails as read and deletes nothing.

Sender check: whether a sender counts as verified (SPF/DKIM/DMARC passed for the From domain) is read from the Authentication-Results header. The sender can put one in the message too – so only the topmost header with the id from INBOUND_MAIL_AUTHSERV_ID counts. Without the variable no sender counts as verified: workflows set to Verified senders only then never start, the default (all but failed ones) keeps running. The id is at the start of the header your server writes into received e-mails (Authentication-Results: mx.example.com; spf=pass …).

en.heading: Integrations
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning

FLOWPLAN_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE empty true allows webhooks to internal addresses and http:// – such as Home Assistant or n8n in the same network. Without this variable only public HTTPS addresses are allowed.
SPACE_GIT_EXPORT empty true turns on the Git export of spaces: space owners push their space into a repository of their own, daily or weekly.
