Space A section in the sidebar, e.g. "Teamspace" or "Private". Open to all members or private.
Page Document, database, whiteboard, journal or dashboard. Pages can have sub-pages at any depth.

en.heading: Page types
paragraphs: – Document: text made of blocks – headings, lists, tasks, tables, code, formulas, diagrams, embeds. See Documents and the editor.
– Database: records with properties, shown as a table, board, calendar, timeline, gallery, list, feed, chart or form. See Databases.
– Whiteboard: an infinite canvas with sticky notes, shapes, connectors, pen and frames. See Whiteboards.
– Journal: one page per day, open tasks move along. See Journal.
– Dashboard: tiles with metrics, charts, database views, tasks due and notes. See Dashboards.
– Workflow: a flow of trigger, logic and actions that runs in the background. Guests do not see workflow pages. See Workflows.

en.heading: Page actions
paragraphs: The … menu at the top right of every page offers:
Action Effect
Change icon, change cover Emoji, symbol or your own image; upload a cover image or choose an existing one and set its position.
Full width The content uses the whole window width.
Change font Default, serif or mono for this page.
Lock page Protects against accidental changes until someone unlocks it.
Duplicate A copy including sub-pages, databases and files; internal links point to the copies.
Move Below another page, into another space or workspace.
Save as template See Templates.
Export, print / PDF See Import, export and versions.
Present Show a document as full-screen slides, see Present.
Open a page beside it … Open a second page on the right in the split view.
Owner and review … Who looks after the page and when it should be checked again, see Owner and review date.
Version history Compare and restore earlier states.
Move to trash Removes the page with its sub-pages; restorable.

en.heading: Right-click in the sidebar
paragraphs: Right-clicking a page in the page tree or under favourites – a long press on a phone – opens its actions directly: Open in new tab, Open in split view, Copy link, Add to favourites, Share, Add sub-page, Change icon, Duplicate, Move, Export, Lock page and Move to trash. Actions with a dialog open the page first.

en.heading: Filter pages
paragraphs: The Filter pages field above the page tree hides everything that does not match; parent pages of the hits stay visible and expanded. Esc clears the filter. Templates, media, tags, graph, trash, settings, help and administration sit as a toolbar at the bottom of the sidebar. On a phone they are gathered behind More next to your name: a tap opens a list of all of them with labels, and the page tree keeps its height.

en.heading: Split view
paragraphs: Two pages side by side – say notes on the left and the task database on the right. A page opens on the right with:
– Open in split view in the right-click menu of a page in the page tree,
– ⌘-click (Windows/Linux: Ctrl-click) on a page in the page tree, under favourites or on a page link in the text,
– dragging a page from the page tree to the right edge of the window (a drop area appears there),
– ⌘ ⌥ S or Open a page beside it … in the … menu: the quick search opens the chosen page on the right.

Each half has its own header with the title and ×. The × on the left closes the left page and the right one moves into the main view; the arrow on the right brings the right page into the main view. Documents can be edited in both halves; databases, whiteboards and dashboards work as usual.

Drag the divider between the halves with the mouse; with the keyboard, tab to it, then ← / → (with ⇧ in large steps), Home / End for the narrowest and widest position, Enter or a double-click for half and half. The device remembers the width.
Dragging a page from the page tree into a document in the other half inserts a link to it there; selected text and blocks can be dragged between the two documents (they are copied).
The right page is part of the address (?split=…): reloading and bookmarks keep the split view. Windows up to 1024 pixels wide and phones do not have it – there, the same ways open the page as usual.
[!NOTE] Since ⌘/Ctrl-click in the page tree now opens the split view, a multiple selection starts with ⇧-click or the tick icon of the space; after that, ⌘/Ctrl-click adds more pages too.

en.heading: Arrange and move
paragraphs: – Reorder pages in the sidebar by drag and drop, or drag them onto another page to nest them. On touch screens a handle only picks something up after a short hold (about 0.3 seconds, with a short vibration); swiping before that scrolls the page, and a quick tap works as usual. The same goes for blocks in a document, home page widgets and records, cards and columns in databases. With a mouse or pen it starts right away.
– Select pages (the tick icon on a space) or ⇧-click marks several pages that can be moved or deleted together.

– Moving to another workspace takes sub-pages, database records and files along. Shares with groups or people who are not members there are dropped. Databases with relations to databases staying behind have to be detached first.

– Moved to another space (or workspace), pages keep the tags and properties of the whole workspace. If they (or their sub-pages and the records of their databases) carry tags or properties that apply only in their current space, a step Bring tags and properties along asks for each one:
– Map to a tag or a property of the same type at the destination – the one with the same name is suggested if there is one,

– Copy to “destination” – a tag or property of its own in the destination space, with all values (the default when there is nothing of the same name there; if the name is taken there, the copy gets the old space's name added, e.g. “Phase (Sales)”),
– Remove – the values are lost then.

Without this choice nothing moves – not by drag and drop, not when moving several pages, not through the API: values are never dropped silently. Undo brings the pages back and maps their tags to the ones of the same name in the old space again. The originals in the old space stay.
[!NOTE] Pages keep their address when moved. Links to the page keep working as long as the reader has access in the new workspace.

en.heading: Owner and review date
paragraphs: So that guides, policies and knowledge pages do not go stale unnoticed, every page can have an owner and a review date. Set both under … → Owner and review … (edit rights needed):
– Owner: a member of the workspace (not a guest) who can read the page.
– Next review on: a fixed date, once, or
– Then every … days: a rhythm such as 30, 90, 180 days or yearly. Without a date it starts today.

Once the review date has come, the page shows the hint “This page is waiting for a review (owner: …)” at the top. Reviewed moves the date on by the rhythm, counted from today; a one-off date disappears. The owner gets a reminder on the due day (““Title” is waiting for your review”) – once per review date, in the inbox and, depending on the settings, as push or e-mail (kind “Date reminders”).
[!NOTE] Through the API, the commands page.owner and page.review set owner and review date. A restore archive keeps review date and rhythm but not the owner, who belongs to the old workspace.

en.heading: Aliases
paragraphs: Under … → Aliases … a page gets further names, such as abbreviations ("PAC" for "Chauffage"). Up to 10 aliases of up to 100 characters each; Enter or a comma separates them, duplicates are dropped. Everyone with edit rights may change them.

@ mentions, the quick search and Unlinked mentions find the page by its aliases like by its title; hits show "Title · alias". When you pick a hit found by an alias in an @ mention, the alias becomes the link text. The Markdown export writes aliases as frontmatter (aliases: [PAC]) at the top of the page – only for pages that have some. Records use the property type Aliases; a page that becomes a record takes its aliases there, and the other way round.
[!NOTE] Through the API, the command page.aliases ({ pageId, aliases: [...] }) sets the aliases of a page; an empty list removes them. A restore archive keeps them.

en.heading: Tags and properties
paragraphs: Every page – document, database, whiteboard, notebook, dashboard, journal day – can carry tags and properties. A tag “Customer” is the same on every page it applies to; a property “Status” has the same options everywhere there. Whether they apply in the whole workspace or only in one space is their scope. (The properties of database records are separate, see Properties, formulas and rollups.)
A slim bar under the page title holds them:

– + Tag opens a field that suggests the tags that apply to the page (the workspace's and those of its space; a space's tags with a small folder icon). ↑/↓ choose, Enter adds, Esc closes. If the name does not exist yet, Create “name” in this space (Enter) creates the tag for the page's space; owners can create it for the whole workspace instead. The field stays open so you can add several tags in a row. The ✕ on a tag removes it from the page.
– Clicking a tag opens the tag view with all pages that carry it.

– + Property lists the properties that apply to the page and that it does not have yet; owners of the workspace and of the space can also choose New property … there – with the choice Only in this space (the default) or In the whole workspace (workspace owners only). You edit values right in the bar – with the same fields as in databases. The ✕ next to a value removes it.
With neither tags nor values the bar is just a faint line with + Tag and + Property; in reading mode, without edit rights and on locked pages it is hidden then.

en.heading: Collapsing the bar
paragraphs: With many tags and properties the bar gets long. The arrow at its far left collapses it into one line: the first tags as small chips (two on a phone, three otherwise), “+3” for the rest and the number of properties, e.g. “6 properties”. Clicking the line – or Enter/Space while it has focus – expands the bar again.

– Your choice is per page and only yours. It is stored in your account, so it applies on all your devices; others keep seeing the page the way they chose. This works in reading mode and without edit rights too.

– Until you choose, the bar is expanded while it is small and collapsed when the page shows more than four properties (properties with a value and the automatic ones such as “Created at” count; empty ones do not). This is decided when the page opens – the bar never folds away while you are filling in values.
– An empty bar (only + Tag and + Property) cannot be collapsed.
– Printing and exports always show all tags and properties, even when the bar is collapsed.
– Guests without an account who open a shared link see no bar, so there is nothing to remember there.

– Through the API the command page.collapseProperties sets your choice: { "action": "page.collapseProperties", "pageId": "…", "collapsed": true } – false expands, null forgets the choice (the rule above applies again).
Property type Value
Text, URL, email, phone Text up to 2,000 characters; URL, email and phone as links
Number a number
Date a day, optionally with a time
Select / multi-select one or several of the defined options
Checkbox yes or no
Person a member of the workspace
Created at, edited at, created by, edited by read from the page automatically
Who may do what:
– A page's tags and values are set by whoever may edit the page – including guests with edit rights on it.
– New tags are created by members with edit rights while tagging – for the page's space. Tags for the whole workspace are created by owners only. Guests and readers only pick existing ones.

– Settings → Tags & properties is changed by workspace owners (everything) and a space's owners (their space's tags and properties); others see the lists. There tags are renamed, coloured (nine colours), ordered, merged and deleted, and properties are created, changed in type and options, ordered and deleted. A changed type or a removed option converts values where possible and removes the others; a deleted property disappears with its values from every page. Renaming, merging and deleting also changes the records of database properties that have the tags as options (see Multi-select with the workspace's tags).
– Values are read by whoever may read the page. The tag view, search and counts only show pages you may read; guests only see the tags and properties of the pages and records shared with them.
Pages in encrypted spaces have no tags or properties – the server would have to store them as plain text.

en.heading: Scope: workspace or space
paragraphs: Spaces separate topics and permissions – tags and properties can too. Every tag and every property applies either
– in the whole workspace – to all pages of all spaces, or
– only in one space – only pages of that space (and the databases in it) use it.

New tags and properties belong to the space you create them in; what existed before this distinction keeps applying to the whole workspace. Lists show the scope with a small label: the space's name (dashed) or “Workspace”.

– Same names: two spaces may each have their own tag “Urgent” – they are different tags. Within what a page sees (its space plus the workspace) a name is unique, ignoring case: a space cannot create a tag “customer” when “Customer” exists for the whole workspace. Same-named items are never merged on their own.
– Visibility: a space's tags and properties are seen by whoever may open that space (and whoever may read a page carrying them), and by the workspace owners.
– Databases with the tags as options offer the tags of their space and of the workspace.

– Settings → Tags & properties filters by scope. A new tag or property gets a scope there (a space's owners: only their space). Merging works only into a tag of the whole workspace or of the same space.
Change scope (arrow icon in the settings, workspace owners only):

– From a space to the workspace (promote) always works. If other spaces have a tag of the same name, the dialog names them; Merge same-named moves their pages to the promoted tag (properties only with the same type) – otherwise everything stays as it is.

– From the workspace to a space (or to another space) first shows where the tag or property is used outside the target space (spaces, pages, records). Then you choose: Copy for the other spaces (each space gets its own tag or property of the same name, with the values), Remove there, or Do not change while it is used there.

[!NOTE] Through the API: tag.save and property.save take spaceId (missing or null: the whole workspace), tag.scope/property.scope change the scope (resolve: block, copy, remove; mergeSameName), meta.usage shows first where something is used. GET /api/tags returns spaceId for every tag and property. See API and webhooks.

en.heading: Tag view
paragraphs: Tags (the tag icon at the bottom of the sidebar, or > tags in quick search) shows all tags with the number of their pages and records. A tag opens the list of its pages, most recently changed first, and below them the records of databases whose multi-select has the workspace's tags as options (with database and space; a click opens the record). Only records you may read appear – no private records of others, no properties hidden from you, nothing behind a journal PIN or in the trash. Above it you narrow the list with text or further tags (“And: + Offer”). A tag is exactly that tag: if other spaces have one of the same name, Also the tag of the same name in another space adds its pages and records. Owners reach the settings through Manage tags. The view has its own address (#tags/) to share or bookmark. In the search, #tag finds the same, see Filter by tags and properties.

en.heading: Copies, templates and trash
paragraphs: Duplicating keeps tags and values (into another space or workspace by name: the ones of the same name there; a space's missing tags and properties are created in the target space). Page templates store tags and values and put them on new pages made from the template; templates of another space ask what becomes of that space's tags and properties. In the trash they are kept and come back on restore; only deleting permanently removes them. Through the API, the command page.properties sets tags and values, see API and webhooks.

en.heading: Favourites and "Linked from"
paragraphs: The star in the header puts a page under Favourites in the sidebar – personal, others do not see your favourites. At the bottom of every page, Linked from shows which pages and database records refer to it.

en.heading: Manage spaces
paragraphs: Via … next to a space → Edit space … or Settings → Spaces:
– rename it, give it an emoji or symbol and one of nine colours,
– switch the visibility between open (all members) and private,
– Duplicate space: an independent copy of all active pages, records and attachments; comments, versions and shares are not copied,
– Git export (only for the owner of the space, when the administration has switched it on): push the space into a Git repository daily or weekly, see Git export of a space,
– move it to the trash. The last active space stays until there is another one.

en.heading: Order of spaces
paragraphs: Workspace owners decide in which order the spaces appear in the sidebar – the same for every member:
– Drag: grab a space by its header (name and symbol) and drop it above or below another space. A blue line shows where it lands.
– Keyboard and phone: … next to the space → Move up or Move down. Screen readers announce the new position.
– Settings → Spaces lists the spaces in the same order, with arrows to move them.
Other members see the new order within a few seconds, without reloading. Wherever spaces are offered for choice – moving, sharing, the browser extension, record to page – the same order applies.
– New spaces go to the end, a duplicated space right after its original.
– A space restored from the trash returns to its old place.
– A restore archive keeps the order of its spaces; on import they go to the end. Older archives without an order keep their previous one.
– Spaces you cannot see – private spaces of others, encrypted spaces without the key – keep their place. Their names appear nowhere; reordering changes nothing about visibility.

[!NOTE] Through the API the command space.reorder ({ workspaceId, order: [spaceIds] }) sets the order of the spaces you see in the sidebar; only workspace owners may do this. The answer lists the visible spaces in their new order.

en.heading: Collapse and expand the sidebar
paragraphs: A click on a space's name collapses its pages or expands them again, and the same works for Favourites and Collections; the arrow in front of a page shows or hides its sub-pages. Pages with sub-pages start collapsed.

Flowplan remembers what you expanded and collapsed – in your account, per workspace, so it is the same on all your devices (browser, phone, desktop app) and after reloading. This covers pages, spaces, favourites, collections and the year and month folders of journals. Others do not see your choice.

– Open page: opening a page expands its space and the pages above it so it is visible in the sidebar; nothing else collapses. This only lasts for the visit – after a reload, only what you expanded yourself stays open (plus the way to the page that is open).
– Expand all / Collapse all: in a space's … menu, for all pages of the space.
– While filtering the page tree, everything with matches is open.
– Deleted pages and spaces drop out of what is remembered.

[!NOTE] Through the API, the command sidebar.state ({ workspaceId, changes: { "": true false } }) saves changes; the keys are p: (expanded), s: (collapsed), g:favorites, g:collections and jo:/jc: for journal folders. The bootstrap returns the state as sidebar.

en.heading: Trash
paragraphs: Deleted pages and spaces end up in the Trash at the bottom of the sidebar, deleted database records below them under Deleted records. Files deleted from Media are listed under Deleted files. There they can be restored or deleted permanently. Publications, share links and forms are switched off when deleting and are not switched on again automatically when restoring.

– Delete permanently next to a page deletes it together with its sub-pages in the trash. The dialog names the page and how many sub-pages go with it. You need the same right as for deleting it: editing the page. Sub-pages you may not edit stay in the trash on their own.

– Empty trash deletes everything in the trash you may delete: pages you may edit, spaces you manage and deleted records you may edit. The dialog shows the counts first. Pages from other people's private spaces and pages you can only read are left untouched.

– Deleted permanently are the page with its content, versions, comments and inline comments, for databases the properties, views and records, plus uploaded files, favorites, publications, share links, notifications and search results. Links from other pages then point to a deleted page. This cannot be undone; a backup is the only way back.

– After 30 days in the trash everything is deleted permanently by itself – pages, spaces, records, files and templates. The line at the top names the period, and every page shows how many days it has left. Admins change the period under Limits & retention (0 = never automatically).

Right after deleting, Flowplan shows a notice at the bottom such as “‘Notes’ moved to the trash” with Undo – for about six seconds, longer while the pointer or the focus rests on it. Undo or ⌘ Z (outside text fields) brings the page back with its sub-pages and opens it again. The same goes for moving pages in the page tree and for several pages at once.

en.heading: Graph of links
paragraphs: The network icon at the bottom of the sidebar (or > graph in the quick search) shows all pages as dots and their links as lines. Database records appear as dots of their own once they link or are linked; a click opens the record. Large dots have many connections; colours tell documents, databases, records, whiteboards and journals apart.
– Drag to pan, scroll or use two fingers to zoom, click to open a page.
– Hovering highlights a page and its neighbours; Highlight marks pages by title.
– Connect sub-pages also shows the page hierarchy (dashed), Pages without links shows or hides single pages.

– Journal days controls the days of journals: hide, one dot per month (default; the dot gathers the links of all days of the month, a click opens the journal) or show each day. The line at the top counts pages and journal days separately.
– Links to pages and records (also from a record's text), embedded whiteboards, linked databases and synced blocks count as connections. The graph only shows what you may see.

en.heading: Unlinked mentions
paragraphs: Below Linked from at the end of a page, Unlinked mentions lists documents and records in which the title of this page appears without being linked (titles of four characters or more), or one of its aliases as a whole word (two characters or more); the alias found is shown in grey next to the hit. Link turns the first mention there into a link to this page, by the title first, else by an alias – the text stays as written. An open record shows the same for its title and aliases below its properties.

Block extensions bring custom block types into the editor: a poll, a counter, a chart from a database, your team's own widget. An extension is a static web page with a manifest. Flowplan shows it isolated in a frame and only talks to it through messages.

en.heading: For owners: register an extension
paragraphs: – Your administrators allow the address: either through PLUGIN_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (configuration) or with the switch Block extensions from any HTTPS address under Administration → Extensions & domains.

– Under Settings → Block extensions enter the address at Address of the extension, e.g. https://plugins.example.org/poll/, and choose Register. Flowplan loads flowplan-plugin.json from there, checks it and shows the extension as a card of its own: which blocks it brings and what it may do, below that the switches Active and Also show on published pages. It is removed with the trash icon at the top of its card.
– In the editor its blocks appear in the / menu under Extensions.
Per extension there is:
– Active – when off, its blocks only show their text.
– Also show on published pages – without this switch its blocks appear on published pages as text only.
– Databases it may read – only when it requests database access.
– Settings – as the manifest describes them. Everyone who sees the block also sees the settings: do not enter passwords.
Registering again reloads the manifest (new version, new block types). Removing it leaves the blocks in the documents; they then show their text.

en.heading: What an extension may do – and what not
paragraphs: The frame has sandbox="allow-scripts" and never allow-same-origin, so the extension runs in an anonymous origin of its own:
– It reads neither Flowplan's cookies nor its storage and cannot change the page around it.
– It knows neither the name nor the e-mail address of the person reading.
– Forms, pop-ups and redirecting the whole page are blocked.
– Every message is checked: sender (exactly this frame), shape (zod schema), the nonce from the handshake. More than 60 messages per second are dropped.
– Height: the extension asks for a height; Flowplan keeps it between 40 px and the manifest's maxHeight (at most 2000 px).
Permissions a manifest can request:
Permission Meaning
read:page Title of the page the block is on.
read:selection The text selected in the editor.
write:block Store its own data in the block (JSON, at most 64 KB) – only for people with edit rights.
read:database: Read records of exactly this database (ID of the database page).
read:database Read records of the databases an owner picks when registering.

Database queries always run with the rights of the person reading: private records and properties with a read rule stay hidden. Published pages never query databases, and blocks there are always read-only.
The text an extension hands over with its data goes into search and the Markdown export. In the export a link to the extension takes the frame's place.

en.heading: For developers: build an extension
paragraphs: An extension is a set of static files served over HTTPS. A complete example (counter and poll) lives in the repository under examples/plugin-hello/.

en.heading: The manifest
paragraphs: flowplan-plugin.json next to the entry page:
"name": "Hello Flowplan",
"description": "A counter and a small poll",
"entry": "index.html",
"blocks": [
{ "type": "counter", "label": "Counter", "icon": "🔢", "description": "A number to count up" },
{ "type": "poll", "label": "Poll", "icon": "📊", "entry": "poll.html" }
"permissions": ["read:page", "write:block"],
"size": { "height": 160, "maxHeight": 600 },
"settings": {
"step": { "type": "number", "label": "Counter step", "default": 1 }
Field Rule
name 1–60 characters.
version 1.2.3, optionally with a suffix (1.2.3-beta.1).
entry Relative path of the page in the frame (default index.html); no .., no other address.
blocks 1–20 block types: type of lowercase letters, digits and -; label; optionally icon (emoji), description and an entry of its own.
permissions See above.
size Initial height and maxHeight in pixels (40–2000).
settings Up to 20 settings: string, number or boolean with label and default.
The manifest must not redirect to another address and may be at most 64 KB.

en.heading: Security headers
paragraphs: Serve the page with a strict Content Security Policy, for example:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'
connect-src 'none' makes sure block data does not leave the frame. If the extension needs a server of its own, name it there explicitly.

en.heading: The message protocol
paragraphs: All messages are objects with protocol: "flowplan-plugin/1". After loading, Flowplan sends:
{ protocol: "flowplan-plugin/1", type: "init", nonce, blockType, readOnly, permissions, settings }
From then on every message of the extension carries this nonce. Answer with ready first; Flowplan then sends the stored data as data.
From the extension Fields Answer
ready – data with the stored data
resize height – (the height is capped)
getData id response with result = data
setData id, data, optionally text (search text, up to 2000 characters) response; errors read-only, permission:write:block or too-large
getContext id response with theme, locale, readOnly, blockType, page.title (with read:page), selection (with read:selection)
query id, databaseId, optionally limit (1–200) response with fields and rows; errors public or permission:read:database:
Answers look like { protocol, nonce, type: "response", id, ok: true, result } or { …, ok: false, error }. When others change the data (simultaneous editing, undo), data arrives again.
A minimal example:
const PROTOCOL = "flowplan-plugin/1";
let nonce = null;
const send = (message) => parent.postMessage({ protocol: PROTOCOL, nonce, ...message }, "*");
addEventListener("message", (event) => {
if (event.source !== parent || event.data?.protocol !== PROTOCOL) return;
const message = event.data;
if (message.type === "init" && !nonce) {
nonce = message.nonce;
send({ type: "ready" });
} else if (message.nonce === nonce && message.type === "data") {
document.body.textContent = JSON.stringify(message.data);
send({ type: "resize", height: document.documentElement.scrollHeight });
Messages to Flowplan go out with the target "*": the frame has no origin of its own that Flowplan could name. Flowplan recognises senders by the frame and the nonce.

en.heading: Try it
paragraphs: – Serve examples/plugin-hello/ over HTTPS (for example behind your reverse proxy).
– Set PLUGIN_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://plugins.example.org and restart Flowplan.
– As an owner register https://plugins.example.org/plugin-hello/ and type /counter in the editor.

Instead of SQLite, Flowplan can use a PostgreSQL database – when you already run a well-kept database server, when more people work at the same time, or when you want several instances in cluster mode.

en.heading: SQLite or PostgreSQL?
paragraphs: SQLite stays the default and is the best choice for most instances: one container, one data folder, nothing else to run. A single query is even faster on SQLite, because it runs inside the same process.
PostgreSQL pays off when
– you already run or rent a database server (with its own monitoring, replication and point-in-time recovery) and want Flowplan on it,
– regularly more than about 20 people work in Flowplan at the same time (see Sizing),
– you want to run several Flowplan instances behind a load balancer – cluster mode requires PostgreSQL.
Feature-wise there is no difference: every feature, search and backups work with both databases. You can switch at any time, in both directions, see Switching the database.

Flowplan still needs its data folder (/app/data) with PostgreSQL: it holds uploaded files (without S3), secrets.key, the push keys and temporary files of backups. Only the database moves to PostgreSQL.

en.heading: Requirements
paragraphs: – PostgreSQL 16 or newer, an empty database (or an empty schema) and a role that owns it. Flowplan needs no superuser rights – and should not have them, see Role without superuser rights.

– A UTF-8 locale such as en_US.utf8 or de_DE.utf8 – the official postgres image and most managed services use one. With the C locale, search still finds Chinese and Japanese text correctly, but much more slowly.

– The pg_trgm extension for full-text search. It ships with every regular PostgreSQL and is "trusted": Flowplan installs it itself into a schema of its own, flowplan_ext, if the role may create objects in the database (CREATE privilege, which the database owner has). Otherwise run CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm; once as an administrator. Without pg_trgm search keeps working, but scans every entry each time (the log says so).

– Optionally pgvector for semantic AI search. From pgvector 0.8 on, Flowplan installs it itself like pg_trgm. Before 0.8 the extension is not "trusted" – an administrator then runs CREATE EXTENSION vector; once in Flowplan's database, and Flowplan uses it from its next start. Without pgvector, Flowplan computes semantic search itself, as on SQLite; switch it off with FLOWPLAN_PGVECTOR=off.

– For backups, pg_dump and pg_restore of at least the server's major version. The Docker image ships the PostgreSQL 18 tools; they back up and restore on servers from version 16 to 18. Without Docker, install a matching postgresql-client package or point FLOWPLAN_PG_BIN at the folder holding the programs.
-- as an administrator (superuser) on the PostgreSQL server
CREATE ROLE flowplan LOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE PASSWORD '<password>';
CREATE DATABASE flowplan OWNER flowplan;
-- in the new database, the extensions into a schema of their own:
\c flowplan
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS flowplan_ext AUTHORIZATION flowplan;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm SCHEMA flowplan_ext;
-- optional, for semantic search (the only way before pgvector 0.8):
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector SCHEMA flowplan_ext;

en.heading: Role without superuser rights
paragraphs: Let Flowplan connect with a role that owns the database but is not a superuser. Flowplan creates and alters tables, functions and triggers in its database – owning it is enough for that. A superuser, on the other hand, can read files on the database server and run programs there (COPY … TO PROGRAM); a flaw in Flowplan, or an administrator exploiting one, would reach the host.

Many images and charts make the configured user a superuser – the official postgres image does so with POSTGRES_USER. In that case create a role of its own as above. The administrator best installs the extensions right away, into the schema flowplan_ext: Flowplan uses an installed extension wherever it is, and otherwise creates pg_trgm (and pgvector from 0.8) in flowplan_ext itself. pgvector before 0.8 can only be installed by an administrator; without it semantic search runs more slowly.
An existing role that is a superuser is demoted by another superuser:
-- once, while flowplan is still a superuser (as flowplan):
CREATE ROLE admin LOGIN SUPERUSER PASSWORD '<password>';
-- then as admin:
ALTER ROLE flowplan NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEROLE NOCREATEDB;
The database and its tables stay owned by flowplan, and the extensions installed so far stay usable. Keep the admin login for administration; Flowplan does not need it.

en.heading: Setting it up
paragraphs: DATABASE_URL selects PostgreSQL. If the value starts with postgres:// or postgresql://, Flowplan uses PostgreSQL; without it, it stays on SQLite.
DATABASE_URL=postgres://flowplan:<password>@db.example.internal:5432/flowplan
# with TLS to the database server:
# DATABASE_URL=postgres://flowplan:<password>@db.example.internal:5432/flowplan?sslmode=require
Special characters in the password (@, :, /, # …) must be percent-encoded in the address, e.g. %40 for @.

On its first start, Flowplan creates all tables, indexes and triggers itself. On every update it adds what the new version needs – it never drops anything, and several instances coordinate through a lock. So an update works as usual: pull the new image, restart the container.

en.heading: With Docker Compose
paragraphs: An example of a single container with PostgreSQL next to it. For pgvector, use the image pgvector/pgvector:0.8.0-pg16 instead of postgres:16.
services:
flowplan:
image: ghcr.io/yannicschuller/flowplan:latest
env_file: .env
environment:
FLOWPLAN_DATA_DIR: /app/data
DATABASE_URL: postgres://flowplan:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@postgres:5432/flowplan
ports:
volumes:
- flowplan-data:/app/data
depends_on:
postgres:
condition: service_healthy
restart: unless-stopped
postgres:
image: postgres:16
environment:
POSTGRES_USER: postgres
POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD}
FLOWPLAN_DB_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
volumes:
- postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
- ./postgres-init.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/10-flowplan.sh:ro
healthcheck:
test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U flowplan -d flowplan"]
interval: 5s
retries: 20
restart: unless-stopped
volumes:
flowplan-data:
postgres-data:

POSTGRES_PASSWORD (the password of the role flowplan) and POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD (that of the image's superuser postgres, for administration only) go into the .env next to compose.yaml (openssl rand -hex 24 each). The script postgres-init.sh from the cluster example creates the role flowplan without superuser rights on the database's first start, gives it the database flowplan and installs the extensions into flowplan_ext – put it next to compose.yaml. A volume made with an older version of this example (POSTGRES_USER: flowplan) keeps its roles: there flowplan is the superuser until you demote it.

en.heading: Variables
paragraphs: Variable Default Meaning
DATABASE_URL empty (SQLite) Address of the PostgreSQL database, postgres://… or postgresql://….

DATABASE_SESSION_URL DATABASE_URL A connection of its own for notifications, the lead in a cluster and pg_dump/pg_restore/psql – only needed when DATABASE_URL points at PgBouncer in transaction mode (below).
FLOWPLAN_PG_SCHEMA public Schema inside the database, if Flowplan shares the database with something else. Created if missing.
FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL 10 Connections per instance (1–500).
FLOWPLAN_PG_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT 120000 Longest a query may run, in milliseconds; 0 = no limit.
FLOWPLAN_PG_LOCK_TIMEOUT 10000 Longest a query waits for a lock (ms).
FLOWPLAN_PG_IDLE_TX_TIMEOUT 60000 A transaction idle this long is ended (ms).
FLOWPLAN_PG_CONNECT_TIMEOUT 30000 Longest a request waits for a free connection from the pool (ms).
FLOWPLAN_PG_PREPARE on off sends every query unnamed instead of as a named prepared statement – for PgBouncer in transaction mode before 1.21 or without max_prepared_statements.
FLOWPLAN_PG_SCHEMA_AUTO on off: the instance does not create or update the schema itself – a separate step does (node /app/scripts/db-schema.mjs, see cluster mode).
FLOWPLAN_PGVECTOR on off ignores pgvector even when it is installed.
FLOWPLAN_BACKUP_FORMAT pg_dump sqlite: scheduled backups in the portable SQLite format instead of pg_dump (below).
FLOWPLAN_PG_BIN empty Folder with pg_dump, pg_restore and psql if they are not on the PATH.
Every variable is also listed, with comments, in the repository's .env.example.
Long-running work such as backups, restores and schema changes lifts the time limits for itself.

Connections: each instance opens up to FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL connections plus up to two of its own (notifications, and in a cluster the election of the leading instance). The server's max_connections must therefore be at least instances × (FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL + 2) plus a reserve for backups and administration. PostgreSQL's default of 100 is plenty for one instance with the default pool.

en.heading: Search on PostgreSQL
paragraphs: Search on PostgreSQL returns the same hits in the same order as on SQLite: parts of words ("plan" in "Projektplanung"), Chinese and Japanese text without spaces, umlauts and accents, title before text, the same snippets. Under the hood it uses trigram indexes from pg_trgm.

[!NOTE] First start after the update or switch: Flowplan builds the two search indexes while it opens the database. On large instances this can take a few minutes, and the instance does not answer meanwhile. Give health checks enough time (start_period, startupProbe). After that, the index fills up in the background – search already works and finds more as it goes.
To rebuild the search index completely, e.g. after installing pg_trgm or when hits are missing:
docker compose exec flowplan node /app/scripts/db-search-rebuild.mjs

The script reads DATABASE_URL and FLOWPLAN_PG_SCHEMA from the container's environment; the running instance then indexes everything again (pages, records, comments, messages and files). The same command works on SQLite.

en.heading: Backups with pg_dump
paragraphs: On PostgreSQL, the scheduled backup and Back up now (Administration → Storage & backup) write a pg_dump archive in custom format: flowplan-2026-11-07-03-00.dump, encrypted as .dump.enc with FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Everything else stays as with SQLite:
– Targets: S3 under /backups/, SFTP or the data folder – with the same retention and the same delayed deletion of files.
– Encryption as before; decrypt.mjs also decrypts .dump.enc.

– The archive holds only Flowplan's schema, without the search index and the pgvector table – Flowplan rebuilds both after a restore. That keeps it smaller, and it restores on a server without pg_trgm or pgvector as well.
– pg_dump runs outside Flowplan and barely loads the instance.

Falling back to SQLite: if no suitable pg_dump is available (too old or not installed), the scheduled backup writes a portable SQLite file (flowplan-….sqlite) instead and notes this in the log. With FLOWPLAN_BACKUP_FORMAT=sqlite it always does. Such a file restores on SQLite and PostgreSQL.

The instance backup (Administration → Storage & backup → Whole instance → Download) always holds the database in the portable SQLite format, so it restores on both databases. Litestream does not run with PostgreSQL – for continuous backups to any point in time, use your database server's own means (WAL archiving, your provider's point-in-time recovery).

en.heading: Restoring
paragraphs: – A pg_dump archive on a running instance (flowplan-….dump, .dump.enc): upload it under Administration → Storage & backup → Restore from backup. Flowplan checks it right away and applies it on the next restart – in cluster mode the leading instance does, see Known limits. Only the database is replaced; the files stay as they are.
– On a new instance with PostgreSQL, the same works on the setup screen: upload it or fetch it from S3 or via SFTP, as in Restore while setting up.
– An instance on SQLite refuses such archives – use the instance backup or switch the database.

– Flowplan checks the archive first (a Flowplan database, not from a newer version), then replaces the whole schema in one transaction and rebuilds the search index. Only the data of Flowplan's tables comes from the archive; tables, functions and triggers are created by the running version itself. Older archives therefore fit into the current tables.

– If the archive holds objects Flowplan does not create itself – custom functions, views, triggers or rules in Flowplan's schema –, Flowplan refuses it: “The backup contains database objects Flowplan does not create itself (such as functions or triggers), so it is not restored.” Keep custom objects in another schema; Flowplan's pg_dump does not back that up. The previous state is kept as pre-restore-/flowplan.dump in the data folder – leave room for one more archive. If the restore fails, the previous state comes back.
– An archive from another schema (FLOWPLAN_PG_SCHEMA) restores as well.
– The instance backup (ZIP) is restored in the same place as before; it fits both databases.

en.heading: PgBouncer
paragraphs: Flowplan pools its connections itself; connecting straight to the server is the simplest way. PgBouncer in front should work as follows – it has not been tested against a real PgBouncer yet:

– Named prepared statements: Flowplan uses them by default. In transaction mode, PgBouncer needs version 1.21 or newer with max_prepared_statements above 0 for them. Otherwise set FLOWPLAN_PG_PREPARE=off: Flowplan then sends every query unnamed (costs about a third of the throughput).

– A session of its own for notifications, the lead and backups: LISTEN, the leading instance's lock in a cluster, and pg_dump, pg_restore and psql need a connection to themselves. They use DATABASE_SESSION_URL – point it straight at the server or at a pool in session mode. Without it they use DATABASE_URL.

– Startup parameter options: Flowplan passes the schema (search_path) and time limits as options when connecting. If PgBouncer refuses it, ignore_startup_parameters = options helps – then the schema must be public, and you set the time limits on the role (ALTER ROLE flowplan SET statement_timeout = '120s' and so on).
# pool through PgBouncer in transaction mode, own sessions straight to the server
DATABASE_URL=postgres://flowplan:<password>@pgbouncer:6432/flowplan
DATABASE_SESSION_URL=postgres://flowplan:<password>@postgres:5432/flowplan
# only without max_prepared_statements or before PgBouncer 1.21:
# FLOWPLAN_PG_PREPARE=off

en.heading: Next
paragraphs: – Switching the database: from SQLite to PostgreSQL and back.
– Cluster mode: several instances with Redis and S3.
– Sizing: how many people an instance carries.
Tools for teams that work with tickets – all optional: a database behaves as before until you set one of them up.
Most of them sit in the … menu on the right of a database's toolbar: record templates, Automations, Status rules and done, Time report and Git connection.

en.heading: Ticket numbers
paragraphs: A property of the type ID (ticket number) shows a running number for every record, such as WEB-123.
– You choose the prefix when adding the property; it is unique in the workspace.
– Numbers are never handed out twice, not even after deleting. A restored record keeps its number.
– In text, WEB-123 is highlighted in every document: hovering shows title and status, ⌘/Ctrl-click opens the record. This also works for text written before the ID property existed.
– Search finds records by their number, and Git commits can refer to them (see below).

en.heading: Subtasks and epics
paragraphs: The type Parent record (subtasks) lets records sit below another record of the same database – for example epic → story → task. Flowplan refuses loops.
– In the record, the Subtasks section lists everything below it with its state; you add new subtasks right there.
– In tables, View → Show subtasks as a tree indents records and lets you fold them.
– Subtask progress is a property of its own: it shows the share of done work across all levels as a bar.
– On boards, Swimlanes by with the parent property gives epic swimlanes.

en.heading: When is a record done?
paragraphs: Sprints, progress, overdue records and “My tasks” need to know when a record is done. Flowplan detects it:
– from a status select with an option like “Done” or “Erledigt”,
– otherwise from a “Done” checkbox.
Set it under … → Workflow and done when it should be different.

en.heading: Status rules
paragraphs: In the same dialog, switch on Set allowed changes and required properties:
– Allowed changes: in the “from (row) to (column)” table, untick changes such as “Open → Done”. A record then has to be “In progress” first.
– Required properties: a status needs certain properties – e.g. “Done only with a solution”.
– Owners only: some statuses can only be set by people with the owner role on the database.
The rules apply everywhere: table and board, bulk edits, guests and the Git connection. A change that does not fit is refused with an explanation.

en.heading: Automations
paragraphs: … → Automations takes care of recurring steps in the form When … only if … then …:
– When: a record is created, a record arrives through a form, a property changes (optionally to a certain value), a date has passed or it is time according to a schedule (see Scheduled automations).
– Only if (optional): conditions such as “Priority is High” or “Assignee is empty”.
– Then: set properties, notify or apply a template.
– Values for properties can be fixed, or today, now, the person who triggered it or the creator.
– You can notify the person in a person property, the creator, the person who triggered it or a specific member.

– Apply template puts a record template on the triggering record – with its placeholders filled in. Either only if the content is empty (existing text then stays untouched) or append below. Empty properties get the template's values. Each rule applies a template to a record only once – even if the status later goes back and forth.
Suggestions add the usual rules in one click:
– “When Status → Done, set a date”,
– “When the due date has passed, notify”,
– “Assign new form records”,
– “When Status → Approved, apply a template” (when the database has record templates).

Example: When Status changes to “Approved”, only if Company is not empty, then apply the template “Kickoff”. Every approved record gets its kickoff page with the company name and date. Applied templates are recorded in the activity log (row.template.applied).
Each rule can be switched off on its own.

en.heading: Open in canvas: a rule becomes a workflow
paragraphs: When a rule is not enough any more – several steps, waits, approvals, AI, e-mails or other services –, the Open in canvas icon next to the rule opens it as a workflow: a workflow page next to the database with the rule as its draft. The rule keeps running until you activate the workflow; then it is replaced by a reference in the same change (“Extended as a workflow”). So both never run at once, and never neither.
The difference: a rule acts for the database, a workflow runs as the person who activates it – the activate dialog says so.

[!NOTE] Rules run on the server, however a record changes. What a rule changes does not trigger further rules, so rules cannot loop. Flowplan checks overdue records every few minutes; each rule fires once per record and date. Notifications appear as “Database automations” and can be switched off in the settings.

en.heading: Scheduled automations
paragraphs: With the trigger it is time (schedule) a rule creates a new record regularly, for weekly reports, monthly closings or maintenance:

– When: daily or every N days, weekly or every N weeks on a weekday, or monthly or every N months on a day (the 31st becomes the last day in shorter months), each at a time in your time zone. Examples: “Every Monday at 09:00”, “Monthly on day 1”, “Every 3 days”.
– Then: Create a record from a record template (properties and text) or empty. Date fields can be set relative to the run, e.g. “Due: +3 days”; 0 means the same day.
The suggestion “Create a record every Monday at 09:00” sets this up with the default template.

[!NOTE] A scheduled rule runs once per date – also after a restart – and only from the moment it was saved. Dates on which the server was not running are not made up one by one; the latest missed one runs once. The rule creates records on behalf of the person who last changed it; if they lose edit rights or the database is locked, the rule rests. Switching it on or off does not change the person.
Repeating tasks, whose next record only appears once the previous one is done, are set in the record, see Repeating tasks.

en.heading: WIP limits
paragraphs: On a board, View → WIP limits sets a maximum per column, e.g. “In progress: 3”.
– The column header then shows 2/3.
– When it holds more, the column is marked.
– With lock, the column takes no further records – wherever they come from.

en.heading: Sprints
paragraphs: A view of the type Sprints (backlog and planning) plans work in time boxes. Set up sprints adds the “Sprint” property and the first sprint the first time.

– Planning: drag records from the backlog into a sprint – with the mouse by the record, on touch devices hold the ⋮⋮ handle briefly and drag – or use Move to, also on phones. With the keyboard: focus the handle, press Space, choose the section with ↑/↓, Space or Enter drops, Esc cancels.
– A sprint has a name, start, end and goal; + Sprint adds the next one.
– Start and Complete: when completing, choose where unfinished records go – the next sprint or back to the backlog.
– Measure size in: number of records or a number property such as story points.
– Burndown: the running sprint shows the work left per day against the ideal line.
– Velocity: closed sprints show what was committed and what was completed.

en.heading: Time tracking
paragraphs: A property of the type Time tracking adds up the time worked on a record. Optionally it shows an estimate from a number property in hours next to it.
– In the record: Start and Stop – each person has at most one running timer, a new one stops the old one.
– Add time: a duration as 45, 1:30 or 1.5h, with a date and a note.
– Correcting: you delete your own entries; owners can correct everyone's.

– … → Time report: the time report of this database, switchable to the whole workspace (see Time reports and billing). The report across all databases is also under Settings → Time; there the filters carry their labels above the report, two side by side on phones.

en.heading: Time reports and billing
paragraphs: The time report sums up the time entries of a database or of the whole workspace.
– Period: This week (from Monday), This month, Last month or a custom period with start and end date (at most three years). The server's time zone applies.

– Filters: person, database (in the workspace), project, billing status and billable yes/no. Project is the record a record's first relation points to (not the parent relation of subtasks) – such as the project of a task. Records without a relation are listed under No project.

– Group by person, project, record, database, day or week. The totals come first (total, open, billed, not billable and – with hourly rates – the amount), then a bar chart and a table per group. Clicking a bar filters by that person, project or database.
– Time entries: the single entries with date, person, record, project, note, duration and billing status (the first 1000; the export contains all).

– Export: CSV (commas, decimal points) for spreadsheets and scripts, CSV for Excel with semicolons, decimal commas and a BOM, as a German Excel opens it correctly with a double click. Cells a spreadsheet would run as a formula start with an apostrophe.
– Print outputs totals, chart and table (also save as PDF); expanded time entries come along.

Who sees what: everyone sees their own time entries and the entries of others on records they may read. If the permissions of the property (who may read it, see Property visibility) hide the time property from someone, they only see their own time there. Own time on a record that has become private since appears without a title as “Record without access”.

Billing status: every time entry is open, billed or not billable. Whoever may edit the record and the time property changes the status – one by one in the list of time entries, or with Mark as billed for all open entries of the current selection. Entries that are not billable stay as they are, as do running timers. Every change is in the activity log (time.billing).

Hourly rates (optional): workspace owners set a rate per person and/or per project under Hourly rates, plus the currency (e.g. EUR, CHF). A project's rate takes precedence over the person's. Members with edit rights in the workspace see amounts; readers and guests see hours only.

Through the API: GET /api/time-reports with page or workspace and the same filters (format=csv or format=excel for the files), POST /api/time-reports with { "action": "billing", "status": "billed", "filter": { … } }.

en.heading: Git connection
paragraphs: … → Git connection connects the database to GitHub, GitLab or Gitea/Forgejo:
– Set up Git connection creates a webhook address and a secret.
– In the repository, add a webhook with both:
– content type JSON,
– events for pushes and pull or merge requests. The exact steps are in the dialog.

– Commits and pull requests that mention a ticket number of this database like WEB-123 appear in the record under Development. Numbers of other databases are left alone – they have their own connection.
– “closes WEB-123” (also fixes, resolves) marks the record done. This happens once the commit is on the default branch or the pull request is merged – through the database's workflow and automations.
Every request is checked against the secret. Only people who may edit the database see the address and the secret. New address and secret invalidates the old ones.
Pull requests show their state as a badge: Open, Merged or Closed.

en.heading: Back-link on the pull request
paragraphs: Like Notion, Flowplan can link back to the record in the pull or merge request itself. In the dialog, under Back-link on the pull request → Add access token, enter the provider, the server (empty for github.com or gitlab.com, required for Gitea/Forgejo) and an access token:
– GitHub: fine-grained token with access to the repository and Pull requests: Read and write (or Issues: Read and write).
– GitLab: project or personal access token with the scope api (role at least Reporter).
– Gitea / Forgejo: token with write:issue (plus read:repository for private repositories).

When a pull/merge request names ticket numbers of this database, Flowplan writes one comment, e.g. Linked in Flowplan: WEB-123 Login form – one line per record, with a link to the record. Later events (edited title, merged, closed) update the same comment instead of writing new ones; if all numbers are gone, it says “No longer linked in Flowplan.”
– The comment shows the ticket number and title. For private records and databases behind a journal PIN, only the ticket number; nothing is written for databases in the trash or in encrypted spaces.

– The token is stored encrypted, never shown again and only sent to the server it was entered for. A webhook from another provider or server does not get it. Own servers are allowed by the administrators with ISSUE_SYNC_ALLOWED_HOSTS, as for the issue sync; internal addresses are blocked.

– The comment is written in the background – the webhook answers at once, even when the Git server is slow. Errors (e.g. 403 for a missing permission) show in the dialog under Last back-link failed. Flowplan writes at most 30 comments per minute and connection.
– Without a token nothing changes: Flowplan writes nothing to the repository. Remove token switches the back-link off.

en.heading: Sync GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo issues
paragraphs: A database can keep itself in step with the issues of a GitHub, GitLab or Forgejo/Gitea repository – both ways or only one. Unlike the Git connection, which only links commits and pull requests, records and issues are created and updated on both sides here.
Setting up the connection (workspace owners and administrators):
– Settings → Calendars & issues → Connect GitHub, GitLab or Forgejo.

– Choose the provider; for an own server enter its address (empty for github.com or gitlab.com), the repository (owner/name) or project (group/project) and an access token that may read and write issues – on GitHub a fine-grained token with Issues: Read and write, on GitLab a token with the api scope. For Forgejo / Gitea the server address is required (e.g. https://codeberg.org); create the token there under Settings → Applications → Generate token with write:issue and read:repository (read:organization optional, so organisation labels are found too).
– Test connection makes one call with the token; Save stores the token encrypted. It is never shown again.
– Optional People: one login = e-mail of a member per line. Assignees are matched through it.

– For immediate updates, add the shown webhook address with the secret in the repository – on GitHub with content type JSON and the events Issues and Issue comments, on GitLab as Secret token with Issues events and Comments, on Forgejo/Gitea under Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook → Forgejo (or Gitea) with POST, content type application/json, the secret and the custom events Issues and Issue comments. Without a webhook, Flowplan syncs every 10 minutes.

The sync acts as the person who set up the connection: they need edit rights on the database, and records they may not read are skipped. If they are no longer an owner of the workspace, the connection pauses until someone saves the token again.
Mapping a database: … → Sync issues in the database. There you choose the connection, repository and direction (both ways, only issues → database, only database → issues) and map properties:
Issue Property
Title Title
Description (Markdown) a text property or the record's document
Open/closed and labels a select – per option "open" or "closed", optionally with a label (e.g. Doing → open + in progress)
Labels a multi-select (only labels that exist as options)
Assignee a person (through the connection's people list)
Milestone due date a date (an existing milestone with that date is set)
Number and address number/text or URL – read-only

Two switches handle comments: issue comments appear as record comments (with name and link), and record comments go out as issue comments. Also take over existing issues fetches all existing issues on the first run; otherwise only what changes after saving. New records become issues once the mapping is saved – older records stay as they are.

Conflicts: if both the record and the issue changed since the last sync, the later change wins. The decision is written to the audit log. Each record is linked to at most one issue; the record then shows a chip like GitHub #123 with a link.

Status: the dialog shows the last pull and push, conflicts, skipped records and errors; Sync now starts a run right away. When the provider reports a rate limit, Flowplan waits for the time it gives. A repository can only be connected to one database. Disconnect ends the sync; records and issues stay.
Pull requests are not synced. Administrators allow own servers (GitHub Enterprise, self-hosted GitLab, your own Forgejo or Gitea) with ISSUE_SYNC_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

en.heading: Records from all databases
paragraphs: My tasks → Records from databases shows records from every database of the workspace in one list. By default these are the open ones assigned to you – through any person property.
– You can filter by due date, database and text.
– Save as view turns a filter into a personal view of its own, e.g. “All my open tickets in all projects”.

en.heading: Import from Jira and Trello
paragraphs: Settings → Import & export → Import → Jira or Trello takes a Jira CSV export (all fields) or a Trello JSON export.
It becomes a new database with a table and a board. It brings over:
– status or list, priority, type, labels, dates and story points,
– assignees – as a person property when they are all members,
– checklists, and parent issues as subtasks,
– descriptions as content and comments as comments,
– attachments as links (the files stay at Jira or Trello).
Relations connect databases, rollups calculate across linked records, formulas calculate values from the properties of the same record.
[!NOTE] This is about the properties of database records. The properties of pages (under the page title) apply in the whole workspace or only in one space, see Scope.

en.heading: Edit properties
paragraphs: A click on the column header or View and properties opens the property dialog: name, type (one of {{facts.fieldTypes}} property types), options and format. Changing the type keeps existing values as far as they fit. Number formats cover currencies, percent, decimal places and thousands separators and also apply to formulas with a numeric result; date fields show short, long or ISO dates and optionally times; Remove date below the field clears it again.

URL, email and phone properties show as links in tables, lists, boards, galleries and records: web addresses open in a new tab (shortened to host and path, the full address in the tooltip), email addresses in your mail app, phone numbers in your phone app. To change one, click the pencil next to the link (on hover or via Tab on a computer, always shown on phones) or the empty part of the cell; Enter saves, Esc discards. Only http:// and https:// addresses, email addresses and phone numbers become links – anything else stays plain text.

en.heading: Rename and merge options
paragraphs: Records store a select or multi-select value as the option's name. When you rename an option in the property dialog, the dialog lists what changes along with it before saving, for example Rename “Open” to “To do” in 12 records.

– Update records carries the new name everywhere: into the records (also record templates, the trash and form drafts), into the views' filters, groups and board columns, into linked views of the database on other pages and into the database's rules – done rule, workflow, automations, form conditions and the issue sync's status mapping. Records keep their value under the new name; workflow checks and automations don't fire for it. Flowplan first keeps a version in the version history.

– Merge: write another option's name in an option's place and the two are merged (Merge “Done” into “Finished”). The records get the remaining option, which keeps its own rules; the merged option's settings under Status rules and done go away – the dialog points this out.
– Save options only saves just the list; records, filters and rules stay on the old names, as before.
– Formulas are not rewritten: if a formula compares against an option's name (such as prop("Status") == "Open"), adjust it yourself.
Renaming needs edit access to the property. For the workspace tags, renaming happens under Settings → Tags & properties.

en.heading: Aliases
paragraphs: The property type Aliases (other names) holds further names of a record, such as "PAC" and "Pompe à chaleur" for the record "Chauffage". A database has at most one such property. In the record you enter the names separated by commas; up to 10 aliases of up to 100 characters each count, surrounding spaces and duplicate names (ignoring case) are dropped.
Aliases work like the title:
– @ mentions and the quick search also find the record by an alias and then show the real title with the alias in grey: "Chauffage · PAC". In the search, aliases weigh as much as the title.
– Unlinked mentions also look for every alias – as a whole word, from two characters, ignoring case. Link keeps the text as written: "PAC" becomes a link to "Chauffage" that still reads "PAC".
– The Markdown export writes them as aliases: into the frontmatter, the Markdown import reads aliases: and alias: back (Frontmatter).

Filters ("contains", "is"), sorting, formulas (as a list, like multi-select), CSV and the other exports treat aliases as a list of texts. An alias may be used by several records; then both appear. Only people who may read a record find it by its aliases.
Pages keep their aliases under … → Aliases … – see Pages and spaces.

en.heading: Property visibility
paragraphs: Single properties such as "Salary" or "Internal note" can be limited to certain people. In the property dialog, the Visibility section sets who may read the property and who may edit it:
Choice Read Edit
Everyone with access (default for reading) Everyone who may read the database –
Editors and owners (default for editing) Edit and owner roles Edit and owner roles
Owners only Owners of the database Owners of the database
Selected groups Members of these groups Members of these groups with edit rights
– Only owners of the database change the visibility; they always see and edit everything themselves.

– Restricted properties show a lock in the column header. Whoever may not read a property does not get the column at all; cells someone may only read are read-only and say on hover who may edit them ("Editable only by …").
– The rules only narrow page and record permissions: whoever may only view the database does not edit a property for "selected groups" either.
– Everyone with access always sees the title property (the first one).

– The server enforces the rules everywhere: in the database itself, in linked views, dashboards, whiteboard cards, exports (Markdown, CSV, JSON, Word, EPUB, print), versions, through the API and the MCP server, for the AI and in calendar subscriptions. It refuses changes to properties someone may not edit – in the record, through bulk editing, import, API, AI or CalDAV – with a message.
– Restricted properties are never public: publications, links with their own permissions, forms, the customer portal and webhooks leave them out, even when a link allows editing.
– Full-text search and the AI's semantic search do not index restricted properties, for anyone.

– Formulas, rollups, AI properties, progress and time that read a hidden property count as hidden for that person as well – their result would otherwise give the value away. A formula with a computed prop() name depends on every property. A rollup is hidden when the person may not read the property in the target database.

– Whoever does not see a property can neither lose nor delete it when changing the schema. Versions of a database with restricted properties are restored by owners only, and records with hidden properties cannot be turned into a page or moved to another database (copying leaves the hidden values out).
Filters and sorting of a view that use a hidden property work on empty values for that person; the condition itself (such as the value compared with) stays stored in the view.

en.heading: Relations
paragraphs: – Add property → Relation and choose the target database.
– Optionally in both directions: the target database gets a counterpart property, and changes are kept in sync on both sides.
– In the cell, search for records and link them; several links can be removed one by one or cleared together.
Relations appear as links in the record. The database search also finds records by the names of linked records, and relation filters offer these names directly.

Linked records show their icon, in the cell and in the picker. Clicking a linked record opens it in a window over the current table – you stay in your database and return to it with Close. Open in database switches to the record's own database.

en.heading: Rollups
paragraphs: – Create a relation first.
– Add property → Rollup, then choose the relation and a property of the target database.

– Choose a calculation – 22 are available, depending on the type: original values, unique values, count, empty/not empty (also as a percentage), sum, average, median, minimum, maximum, range, checked/unchecked, earliest and latest date, date range.

Earliest and latest date over Created at or Edited at give an instant in UTC, shown in your time zone. Number rollups appear as a number, progress bar, progress ring or rating, with an adjustable target value. Values from databases someone may not read are not loaded for that person.

en.heading: AI properties
paragraphs: When AI is switched on, a property can take its value from an instruction to the AI – such as a summary or a category from other properties. Everything about it under AI in databases.

en.heading: Formulas
paragraphs: Choose the type Formula in the property dialog. The editor offers 58 functions with search, categories, signatures and examples, suggestions while you type and a live preview on a record of your choice.
round(prop("Effort") * prop("Hourly rate"), 2)
if(prop("Done"), "✓", concat(format(dateBetween(prop("Due"), today(), "days")), " days"))
– References with prop("Name") stay valid when the property is renamed.
– Syntax errors show their position and prevent saving.
– Numeric results are available in filters, sorting, charts and column calculations.
– Date functions calculate in UTC unless a zone is given; now() and today() update every minute.

– If a date is empty, date functions return an empty result instead of #ERROR. In comparisons an empty value counts as 0 – so dateBetween(prop("Due"), today()) < 3 also matches records without a date; guard it with !empty(prop("Due")) && dateBetween(prop("Due"), today()) < 3.
– Formulas read Created at and Edited at as an instant in UTC (such as 2026-11-05T17:39:02Z), so every date function works with them, e.g. formatDate(prop("Created at"), "MM/DD", "America/New_York").
– Formulas do not run JavaScript; length, nesting and result size are limited.

en.heading: Function groups
paragraphs: Group Examples
Logic if, ifs, coalesce, and, or, not, empty
Numbers sum, average, min, max, round, ceil, floor, abs, mod, pow, sqrt
Text concat, length, contains, replace, replaceAll, trim, slice, lower, upper, format, toNumber
Date now, today, parseDate, formatDate, dateAdd, dateSubtract, dateBetween, year, month, day, hour, timestamp
Lists list, count, at, first, last, join, split, unique, sort, reverse
The formula editor shows the complete list.
The quick search finds content right down into file attachments. The inbox and push notifications tell you when someone needs you.

en.heading: Quick search
paragraphs: ⌘ K (Windows/Linux Ctrl K) or Search in the sidebar.
It searches:
– page titles and aliases as well as document text,
– tags and property values of pages,
– database records and their content,
– comments,
– file names,
– the text of PDF attachments (up to 50 MB, the first 100,000 characters),
– scanned PDFs and images with text recognition (German and English, French or Chinese (Simplified) on request via FLOWPLAN_OCR_LANGS),
– Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OpenDocument files.

Hits can be filtered by type and space. Journal days come after all other hits; Without journal days leaves them out completely and stays on for the next search. File text is indexed in the background and can be found after a few seconds. The search only shows what you may read. Enter opens the first hit.

Aliases of pages and records weigh as much as the title. When the search only matches an alias, the hit shows the real title with the alias in grey, e.g. "Chauffage · PAC". The same applies in the @ mention dialog.

en.heading: Filter by tags and properties
paragraphs: These words act as filters in the search:
Input Finds
#customer pages with the tag “customer” (case does not matter) and database records carrying it in a multi-select with the workspace's tags; tags with spaces as #"New idea"
-#internal leaves out pages and records with the tag
Status:Open property “Status” with the value “Open” (select and multi-select: exactly this option; text, URL, email, phone: contains)
Budget:>1000, Budget:<=50, Budget:10..20 compare numbers
Due:2026-12, Due:>2026-11-01, Due:2026-11-01..2026-11-30 dates: day, month or year; after, between (also =, <=)
Billed:yes / Billed:no checkbox
Owner:Emil, Owner:me person by name; me is you
Status:* / Status:- property set / empty

Names with spaces go in quotes: "Next step":Offer. Several filters apply together; the remaining text is searched as usual. Filters without text list all matching pages, most recently changed first. Records count with their own tags and those of their database page. Words that name no tag and no property (like #123) stay ordinary search words.

Tags and properties can apply in one space only, and two spaces may have ones of the same name. #Urgent is a name: it finds the pages with any tag of that name you may see – in each space the one that applies there. The Tag … choice next to the search field shows, with a space chosen, only its tags and the workspace's; for all spaces all of them with the space's name as a hint. The tag view, in contrast, shows exactly one tag (same-named ones of other spaces on request).

Recognised filters appear as chips under the search field; ✕ removes one. The Tag … choice next to the space adds a tag filter. Collections keep the filters. Tag names and values are also ordinary words of the page: “customer” also finds pages tagged “customer”.

en.heading: Combine: AND, OR, NOT
paragraphs: Conditions combine freely, in the search and in collections:
Input Meaning
#customer #open both (AND; you may write AND between them)
#open OR #waiting, #open \ #waiting either
-#internal, NOT #internal, -draft without; - or NOT works before any condition and before parentheses
(#open OR #waiting) -#internal parentheses group
created_by:Anna, creator:me created by (a name, or me for you)
updated_by:Emil, editor:me last changed by
created:-7d, updated:this-week created or changed in the last 7 days, this week
created:2026-03, updated:>2026-01-01, created:2026-01-01..2026-01-31 year, month or day; after (>, >=), before (<, <=), a range
type:document, type:database\ whiteboard, type:record only documents, databases, whiteboards or database records (also notebook, journal)
in:"Team Marketing" only in this space
title:offer only the title contains the word

Relative dates: -7d, -2w, -3m and -1y mean the last 7 days, 2 weeks, 3 months or a year, including today. You can also use today, yesterday, this-week, last-week, this-month, last-month, this-year and last-year. Weeks start on Monday. "Today" is the day in your time zone. These also work for date properties: Due:this-week.
Precedence: NOT/- binds tightest, then AND, then OR. So #A #B OR #C means (#A #B) OR #C. Use parentheses when in doubt. OR, AND and NOT only count in capitals. A lower-case "or" stays a search word.
Words: Words right next to each other are searched as one phrase, as before. With AND between them (invoice AND open), they can appear anywhere.

Keys: created_by, creator, updated_by, editor, created, updated, type, in and title are English and ignore case. If a property has the same name, put its name in quotes: "Type":Book. For database records, Property:value first checks the record's own property of that name (e.g. Priority:High), then the database page's.

All existing searches work as before. Searches that use the new conditions list the matching pages and records without a text snippet, most recently changed first. The server does not search end-to-end encrypted spaces.

en.heading: Commands
paragraphs: The same quick search also runs commands: if the input starts with >, only commands appear, such as > new database, > tasks, > dark or > focus; Enter runs the first one. Matching commands also appear above the search hits without >. With a page open there are page commands as well: favourite, follow, comments, export, print/PDF, version history, share and focus mode.

en.heading: Collections
paragraphs: A collection is a saved search with its own place in the sidebar. Each time you open it, Flowplan searches again. New and changed pages and records that match appear by themselves.
– Create: In the quick search, choose Save as collection (the search's kind and space become type: and in:), or select + next to Collections in the sidebar.

– Filters or text: In the editor, build the query under Filters. Groups require all conditions (AND) or any condition (OR). You can exclude any condition or group (NOT). The conditions are tag, created by, last edited by, property (by type: select, multi-select, text, number, date, checkbox, person), created and updated (relative or fixed), type, space, title contains and text contains. Text shows the same query in the search language. Both views stay in step: what you change in the text shows up in the filters again. If a text cannot be shown as filters (for example because of a missing parenthesis), the editor stays in text mode and says so. Below the query you see right away how many matches there are.
– Results: As a list or a table with title, type, space, tags, updated and created by. Select a column heading to sort. At most 500 matches are shown, most recently changed first.

– Manage: The … menu next to a collection has Edit (name, emoji, filters, sharing), Duplicate, Move up/Move down and Delete. You can also drag collections into order; the order is yours alone. After you delete a collection, Undo brings it back.
