– Sharing: New collections are private. With Share with the workspace, all members see it under Shared; guests do not. Only you and the workspace's owners can change or delete it. Only you can share it or stop sharing it. Others can choose Duplicate as my collection.

– Permissions: In a collection, each person sees only what they may read themselves. This also applies to shared collections: no private spaces, no private records of others, no hidden properties, no journals behind a PIN, nothing from the trash. End-to-end encrypted spaces are left out, and the collection says so.
– Limits: 100 collections per person and workspace, 100 shared ones per workspace.
Saved searches from earlier versions became private collections when you updated. Searches for comments or files keep their words, but not the kind.

en.heading: Inbox
paragraphs: The Inbox collects:
– mentions,
– comments that concern you (see below) and replies in text comments you took part in,
– date reminders,
– comments and records from guests via share links,
– pages and workspaces shared with you,
– changes on pages you follow (you follow your own pages when creating them; the bell at the top right toggles following),
– messages from automations.

en.heading: Who hears about comments
paragraphs: A new comment – on a page, on a database record or as a new text comment – does not notify the whole workspace, only:
– who follows the page (whoever creates a page follows it automatically; for a record: who follows the database),
– the page's owner,
– for a record: who created it and the people in its person properties (such as Assignee),
– who already commented on the same page or record,

– who is mentioned in the comment with @ – in page and record comments by full name or e-mail address (@Anna Berg). Someone mentioned who would be notified anyway gets a single notification, the mention.

Replies in a text comment reach everyone who has written in that thread and the people mentioned in it. The author and anyone who may not see the page or the record are never notified. To keep up with a page, follow it with the bell.

By default what concerns you directly – mentions, shared pages, comments, reminders – arrives in the inbox, as push, by e-mail and in connected chat apps. Guest comments come without e-mail and chat app. Changes on pages you follow and automations only land in the inbox, so that not every small edit triggers a notification or mail. Under Settings → Notifications this can be changed per kind and channel; Reset to defaults restores the initial state.
Retention: read notifications are deleted after 90 days, unread ones after a year; at most the newest 1,000 per person are kept. The inbox shows the newest 100.

For administrators: security incidents of the instance. Admins see their own row Security incidents of the instance among the notification kinds: what the detection rules find on the whole instance (password guessing, new admin rights, probing …). Each admin chooses how incidents arrive – inbox, push, e-mail and chat apps are on by default – and which: All incidents (default) or Critical only. The choice applies to every channel of this kind; every incident still shows under Administration → Threats & incidents. Clicking or tapping the notification opens the incident's page. The row Security notices is only about your own account (a new sign-in, a wrong journal PIN, a chat app switched off); whoever had switched channels off there before the update has them off for security incidents too. Other people don't see the row.

Unread items are marked and can be filtered. A click opens the spot, for text comments the thread directly. Notifications without a page lead to their place in the app: a security incident to its page under Administration → Threats & incidents, a new sign-in to the signed-in devices, a chat app switched off to its connections – also when tapping the push notification and through the link in e-mails and chat apps.

en.heading: Notifications from workflows
paragraphs: Workflows use two kinds of their own that you can switch off per channel under Settings → Notifications: Messages from workflows (what a workflow sends) and Errors, pauses and approvals of workflows – so you never miss an approval when you mute the messages. An approval notification opens the workflow page on the Approvals tab.

en.heading: E-mail
paragraphs: If a mail server is set up on the instance, unread notifications arrive by e-mail as a digest after ten minutes – one mail for everything that has piled up, each notification at most once. Under Settings → Notifications, the E-mail column can be switched on and off per kind. Invitations to a workspace and pages shared with you arrive by e-mail right away.

en.heading: Weekly digest
paragraphs: Under Settings → Notifications → Weekly digest you subscribe to an e-mail that arrives every Monday at 7 am in your time zone (your browser's time zone is saved when you switch it on):
– Changed in pages you follow – with the workspace and who changed it (changes of the last seven days, by others only),
– Overdue tasks and Open tasks – as in My tasks, across all workspaces.

With a short AI summary of the changes (only shown when AI is on for you) puts a few bullet points before the list. The AI only reads pages it may read for you, with your AI provider. If AI is off or the request fails, the e-mail comes as a plain list. If there is nothing to report in a week, no e-mail is sent. The digest needs a mail server to be set up.

en.heading: Push notifications
paragraphs: Under Settings → Notifications:
– Enable push – the browser asks for permission. This applies per device.
– In the card Notification kinds, set the switches Inbox, Push and E-mail per kind – every change is saved at once. On a phone every kind is a card of its own with three labelled switches.
– Use Send test notification to check that everything arrives (see below).
Push notifications open the page concerned. No document content appears on the lock screen.
[!NOTE] iPhone and iPad (iOS 16.4 or later): open Flowplan in Safari over HTTPS, Add to Home Screen and start it from that icon. Only there can push be enabled.
Signing out, the end of a session or a locked account end the push subscription; enable it again after the next sign-in if needed.

In the apps for iPhone, iPad and Android, notifications come through the app: it asks for permission after the first sign-in, and the number of unread ones shows on the app icon. Notification kinds apply there as well. These notifications are end-to-end encrypted and therefore show their text – the relay, Apple and Google cannot read it, see Push relay.

en.heading: Test notification
paragraphs: Settings → Notifications → Send test notification immediately sends a notification "Test notification – everything works." to all your push targets: every browser with push enabled and every app with notifications allowed. It takes the same way as every notification – Web Push, the push relay or Expo – but leaves nothing in the inbox. Tapping it opens these settings.
After at most ten seconds, each device is listed with the channel it went through (Relay · end-to-end encrypted, Expo or Web Push) and what happened:
– Delivered – handed to Apple, Google or the browser's push service. If nothing shows up anyway, check the device: are notifications allowed for Flowplan? An active Focus is mentioned.
– Registration expired – open the app once, it registers again. For a browser whose subscription expired, enable push there again.
– Notifications turned off – allow them in the app or in the device's system settings.

– Push relay not set up, unreachable or instance not verified – this concerns the instance, not your device; the message gives the reason (e.g. PUSH_RELAY=off, APP_URL without HTTPS, /.well-known/flowplan-push not reachable). See Configuration.
– No devices registered – enable push above or open the app and allow notifications.

The test only goes to your own devices, regardless of Notification kinds and Focus filters – the device's own permission and Focus still apply. At most five tests in ten minutes. The result never shows tokens or keys; administrators also see a diagnostics line with the relay address, whether /.well-known/flowplan-push is enabled and the instance's address (APP_URL).

The desktop app has no Web Push. It asks for new notifications itself and shows them as system notifications, with the unread count on the app icon. There, Settings → Notifications shows a switch for the app's notifications instead of Enable push; Do Not Disturb and All Profiles are in the app's Notifications menu. Notification kinds apply here too: only kinds with push pop up.

en.heading: Chat apps
paragraphs: Instead of (or besides) push and e-mail, notifications arrive right away in a chat app: Telegram, Gotify, ntfy or Matrix. Under Settings → Notifications → Chat apps you connect one target per service; which kinds arrive there you choose in the Notification kinds card, column Chat apps. By default these are mentions, shared pages, comments, reminders and security notices – not guest comments, changes on pages you follow or automations. What is switched off for the inbox does not reach the chat app either.
Service What you enter

Telegram – the instance's bot Nothing: Create a connection link, open the link on the device with Telegram and tap Start (or send the bot /start ). The code is valid for 15 minutes and only once. Only available when the administration has set up a bot.

Telegram – own bot Bot token (from @BotFather), your chat ID (e.g. from @userinfobot) or @channelname, optionally an own API address – for a self-hosted Bot API server or a relay/proxy. Message your bot once so it may write to you.
Gotify Server address and app token (create one in Gotify under Apps). Tapping the notification opens Flowplan.

ntfy Server (empty: https://ntfy.sh), topic, optionally an access token or user and password. On ntfy.sh every topic is public – choose a name that is hard to guess, or your own server with authentication.
Matrix Homeserver, room ID (!abc:example.org, in Element under Room settings → Advanced) and the access token of an account that is in the room – preferably a separate bot account.

Send test message sends a message right away and shows the outcome: delivered, Credentials refused (HTTP 401), Not found (HTTP 404) (address, topic, room or chat ID), Server not reachable or Internal addresses are blocked. Change takes new details; an empty token field keeps the stored token. Disconnect deletes the connection with its credentials.

What a message says: as with push, the kind, a short excerpt of the notification and a link to the place. With Include the text off, only “New notification in Flowplan” with the link. Notifications from end-to-end encrypted spaces always arrive without content. Tokens or other secrets are never part of a message.

Credentials (bot, app and access tokens, passwords) are stored only encrypted, like other stored secrets, and never shown again – only “Token set (…abcd)”. Connecting and disconnecting appear under Settings → Security check → Sign-ins & changes.

Delivery: messages go through a queue like push and e-mail. If the service does not answer, Flowplan retries with growing pauses and gives up after six attempts; if the service throttles (HTTP 429), Flowplan waits as long as asked. At most 20 messages a minute go to one target. What you already read in the app is not sent any more. If the service refuses a target three times in a row (401/403/404 or a blocked internal address), Flowplan switches it off and tells you in the inbox; Switch on again resumes it once fixed.

For administrators: the switch Operations alerts sends failed backups, full storage, errors of background workers and many failed sign-ins (at most once a day per alert) to your chat apps – also without a webhook under Monitoring. Security incidents arrive through the row Security incidents of the instance of the notification kinds, not twice.
Which services and servers are allowed is up to the administration (Administration → Chat apps).

Share at the top right of every page opens Share page. A line at the top sums up how the page is shared right now – space, people, links and whether it is published. Below, three tabs handle one thing each: People (who in the workspace may access it), Links (named links for outsiders; only for those who may do more than read) and Web (publishing). Longer explanations sit behind the small (i). At the bottom, Copy link to page copies the page's address for everyone with access, and Done closes the dialog.

en.heading: Access in the workspace
paragraphs: Pages inherit the permissions of their space and parent pages; below the list, the People tab names who comes in through the space (such as “Plus all 8 members of the space Team”, with Manage space for those who may). In addition, individual people or groups can be given permissions:
Role May
View Read and comment
Edit Change content, records and views
Private spaces and pages are only visible to the people they are shared with. Guests only see what has been explicitly shared with them (see Workspaces, members and permissions).

en.heading: Share a page with a person
paragraphs: A page or database can be shared with someone who is not in the workspace – without taking them into the whole workspace. Share → People: enter an e-mail address (members are suggested), choose View or Edit, Add.

– The person already has an account on this instance (with a confirmed address): they have access to the page and its sub-pages right away and get a notification in the inbox ("… shared “Page” with you") and – when the instance sends e-mail – right away an e-mail with a link to the page. Settings → Notifications → Pages shared with you turns the e-mail off. If they are not in the workspace yet, they join as a guest and see only what is shared with them.

– No account yet: they get an invitation by e-mail (when set up) and are listed as "Invited". Once they create an account with this address, the page is there. The same goes for an account whose address is not confirmed yet – then only the invitation link (Settings → Members → Pending invitations → Copy link) opens the page.
– Guests do not see the list of people with access; only those who may share see e-mail addresses. Each person sends at most a few dozen invitations an hour, and each address gets only a few e-mails.
– In the list, roles can be changed and people removed. A guest without any shared page left is no longer in the workspace either.
– Owners of the workspace and owners of the page's space may share. Everyone else only sees the list.

en.heading: Links with their own permissions
paragraphs: In the Links tab, + New link creates as many named links as you like, e.g. "Feedback from the customer": choose a name and permission, optionally sub-pages, a password and an expiry date, then Create link. Each link in the list has a copy button and a ⋯ menu.
Link permission Visitors may
Read look at the page
Read and comment also comment; comments carry a guest note
Read, comment and edit also change the title, text and visible properties of existing records
– Links work without an account and can be revoked one by one (⋯ → Revoke).
– With edit links, guests write along live: changes by members and other guests appear right away, and cursors are visible both ways – guests appear as "Guest · ".
– Optionally they also apply to the sub-pages that exist right now; new sub-pages are not added automatically.
– Edit links cannot change permissions, members, private relations or files properties. Before every guest edit, Flowplan saves the previous content.
– A journal with a PIN can be neither shared by link nor published; setting the PIN revokes existing links and publications. Sharing a page above it with its sub-pages leaves it out.

en.heading: Password and expiry date
paragraphs: Links with their own permissions and publications can have a password and an expiry date – when creating them or later: for links via ⋯ → Password and expiry date, for the publication in the Web tab under Password and Expires. The list shows "Password" or "expires on …".
– Visitors enter the password once per device. It is valid for up to 12 hours and only for this link; a new password signs all visitors out.
– Ten wrong attempts within 15 minutes block that address for the link.

– Editing links have daily budgets: per link, guests upload at most 200 MB of files per day (20 files per 10 minutes) and send at most 100 MB of changes per day; a document does not grow beyond 3 MB of text through a link. For the whole instance FLOWPLAN_ANONYMOUS_UPLOAD_MB applies on top (Configuration).
– After the expiry date the link only shows "expired" – no content, no files, no live updates.
– You can remove the password or extend the date at any time.
– Password-protected publications cannot be copied into other workspaces.
– The password is stored only as a hash and never shown again.

en.heading: Publish on the web
paragraphs: In the Web tab, the Publish on the web switch makes the page readable for everyone with the link. Then come the public link (Copy or open it) and the options:
– Also publish the current sub-pages; Add new sub-pages to the selection brings in ones created later.
– Visitors may copy it into their workspace – only what the publication shows.

– Databases appear with their views – table, board, gallery, list, feed, calendar, timeline and chart (also with series and more values) –, records and record documents. A view is only published if all properties it needs are public. Person properties, relations, formulas, rollups and internal comments stay private.
– Files linked in published pages are public; other uploads are not.
– Switching it off, deleting or moving a page out of the published tree revokes access immediately, including to files.

– If a page has headings, visitors show its outline with the list icon to the right of the text (on a phone, the round button at the bottom right). It marks where you are reading and jumps to a heading on click. The browser remembers whether it is open – as in the editor.

en.heading: Appearance
paragraphs: In the Web tab, Appearance folds open below the options. There you set the look of the publication: logo and favicon (an HTTPS address or an uploaded file the publication shows), accent colour, footer text and hide “Published with Flowplan” – applied with Save appearance.

en.heading: Custom domain
paragraphs: When the administration switched it on (Custom domains for publications), a publication can also be shown under your domain, such as docs.example.org:
– In the Web tab, open Custom domain, enter the domain and choose Add domain.
– At your DNS provider create the TXT record shown: name _flowplan-verify.docs.example.org, value flowplan-verify-…. Only this TXT record verifies the domain.
– Point the domain at the Flowplan instance with a CNAME (or A/AAAA) record.
– Choose Check now. The reverse proxy obtains the HTTPS certificate – see Custom domains for publications.

A verified domain stays verified until you remove it – including domains verified another way in the past. A domain that is still not verified after 7 days is released again; after that someone else may enter it.

Under the domain there are short addresses (/ for the start page, / for sub-pages), a sitemap.xml and robots.txt of its own, and search engines may index the pages; the /share/… link names them as the canonical address. The domain shows only this publication: no sign-in, no app, no API apart from the publication's read access, no cookies, and the pages cannot be embedded in other sites.
Publications with a password cannot be shown under a custom domain. When the publication ends, the domain answers with 404.
[!WARNING] Embedded videos and external images load content from their provider when viewed. This also applies to published pages.

en.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Forms have a link of their own, see Forms.

Flowplan signs people in with e-mail and password, optionally with passkeys. In addition – or instead – sign-in can go through an OpenID Connect provider (single sign-on), whose groups decide who administers the instance.

en.heading: E-mail and password
paragraphs: Without further setup, the sign-in page shows a form for e-mail and password.
– The first account of a new instance administers it: the sign-in page then offers Create account right away. This account sees the Administration.

– Instances reachable from the internet: until the first account exists, anyone who opens the address could create it and administer the instance. Set FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN to a random value (e.g. openssl rand -hex 24): the first account can then only be created with the setup link https://flowplan.example.com/register?setup=; without it the page offers no sign-up. The token also protects Restore from a backup on the setup screen. Once the first account exists the token has no effect. Without a token and with an APP_URL that does not point to this machine, Flowplan warns at start in the log and with a note on the setup screen. The Helm chart generates the token itself. If two people sign up first at the same moment, only one of them becomes administrator; the other gets a note. With single sign-on you can also never use the link – the administrators then come through the group in OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP, and everyone else joins by invitation.

– Further accounts are created when the administrators open sign-ups under Instance → Allow sign-ups with e-mail and password – or for addresses with an invitation: the invitation link opens the form with the invited address and creates an account only for it; without e-mail it works only through the link. Workspaces someone was invited to appear as soon as the address is confirmed via the e-mail link.

– Confirming the e-mail address: if the instance sends e-mail (SMTP_* set), a new account signs in only after the address has been confirmed with the link from the e-mail – the link signs in right away. Trying earlier shows a notice and sends the link again (at most every five minutes); Send the link again also works after signing up. Without e-mail every account counts as confirmed immediately, as does the instance's first account. Admins can confirm an address by hand under Administration → Users, with Mark as confirmed in the account's side panel; resetting the password via a link confirms it too. If the address already has an account, signing up shows the same as for a new address, and the account's owner gets a note by e-mail instead – so the page does not reveal which addresses have an account.

If you open the confirmation link in a different browser from the one you registered in, you set a new password there – the one chosen at registration no longer works. This way nobody can create and keep an account for someone else's address in advance.

– Passwords have at least 10 characters and are stored with scrypt. After 8 failed attempts for an account from the same IP address (or 30 failed attempts from one IP address in total) that address pauses for 15 minutes. Someone who knows your address cannot lock you out this way: from other IP addresses you still sign in. Against attempts from many IP addresses at once, every sign-in to an account with more than 10 failures in 15 minutes waits a little longer (up to 5 seconds), and after 100 the account is locked for the rest of the 15 minutes. Without a known client address (see FLOWPLAN_TRUSTED_PROXIES) the limit of 8 applies to the account itself. The same holds for signing in with LDAP. These limits – like those for codes, passkeys, confirming important steps and passwords of shared links – hold under many parallel requests too: every attempt counts before the password is checked.

– Forgot password: with e-mail delivery set up, the sign-in page sends a link that is valid for two hours. Without e-mail, the administrators create a link to hand over under Users, with Password → Create link in the account's side panel. After a reset all previous sessions are ended.
– Admin right: under Users, the administrators pass it on (Make admin) or take it away; someone always has to administer the instance.

– Everyone changes their name and password under Settings → Account & security (card Profile, or Change password … in Sign-in & security). The name is saved when you leave the field. After a password change, turning on the authenticator app and removing a passkey, all other sessions end; the current one stays signed in. Starting a demo while signed in signs the previous account out. A wrong current password when changing it counts like a wrong code: too many failures block it for 15 minutes.
– Sign-ups and "Forgot password" are limited per address and network address (at most one reset e-mail every five minutes per account).
FLOWPLAN_LOCAL_LOGIN=false turns off e-mail, password and passkeys – then only single sign-on remains.

Under Settings → Account & security, the Sign-in methods card shows how you sign in: e-mail and password, the directory (LDAP) and connected SSO identities with provider, address, date connected and last use. That is where you connect and disconnect SSO identities and remove or set the password – see Connect an existing account to SSO.

en.heading: Passkeys
paragraphs: With a passkey you sign in with your fingerprint, face recognition or device PIN, without a password. Passkeys are created under Settings → Account & security → Add a passkey; afterwards Sign in with a passkey on the sign-in page is all it takes.

Under Settings → Account & security, the card Sign-in & security lists password, two-factor sign-in, passkeys and the signed-in devices, each with its state (“Off”, “On · 8 codes left”, “2 passkeys”). Delete account is at the very bottom, in the Danger zone. Addresses such as /#settings/account/passkeys or /#settings/account/two-factor open a card directly.
– Passkeys exist for accounts with e-mail and password. SSO accounts sign in with their provider, which may offer passkeys itself.
– Passkeys belong to the domain in APP_URL. They need HTTPS (or http://localhost during development); a bare IP address does not work. Whoever changes the domain creates the passkeys anew.
– A passkey can be removed in the settings at any time.
– In the desktop app, Sign in with a passkey and Sign in with SSO open the sign-in in the default browser and hand it back to the app afterwards (Desktop apps).

en.heading: Two-factor sign-in
paragraphs: Accounts with e-mail and password can add an authenticator app, such as Aegis, 2FAS, Google Authenticator or 1Password.
– Settings → Account & security → Two-factor sign-in → Set up an authenticator app.
– Scan the QR code with the app – or type the key shown.
– Confirm with the current six-digit code.
– Keep the ten recovery codes safe. They are shown only once, and each works exactly once.
When signing in, Flowplan asks for the code from the app (or a recovery code) after the password.
– A code counts only once; codes from the previous and the next 30-second window are accepted, so a slightly wrong clock doesn't matter.
– Too many wrong codes block sign-in for 15 minutes.

– Passkeys are enough on their own: signing in with a passkey needs no code – even with the app turned on. Whoever wants a code as well turns on Also ask for a code after the passkey under Settings → Account & security → Two-factor sign-in → Manage. Turning it off needs the password or a current code.
– SSO accounts get their second factor from the provider; API tokens are not affected.
– Turning it off and new recovery codes need the password or a current code.
– Forgot password does not skip the second step.
– Lost your phone and your codes? An administrator can reset two-factor sign-in (Administration → Users).

Admins can require two-factor sign-in for all local accounts or only for admins (Administration → Sign-in & SSO). Accounts without an app and without a passkey then set up a second factor right after signing in, before using Flowplan; accounts with a passkey but no app sign in with the passkey.

[!IMPORTANT] The apps' keys are stored encrypted – with FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, otherwise FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY, otherwise with the generated file secrets.key in the data folder (Configuration). Be sure to back up this file or the key: the instance backup deliberately leaves it out. Without it, only the recovery codes work after a restore.

en.heading: Single sign-on with OIDC
paragraphs: Optional. With OIDC_ISSUER set, the sign-in page shows Sign in with SSO; new people are created on their first sign-in. E-mail accounts and SSO accounts can exist side by side.

en.heading: Create a client at the provider
paragraphs: Register a confidential web client – or a public client: if OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET is empty, Flowplan signs in without a secret and relies on PKCE alone. That suits providers that serve many instances with one client. Providers that sign ID tokens with the client secret only (HS256) need a confidential client.
Setting Value
Redirect URI https://flowplan.example.com/api/auth/callback
Flow Authorization code with PKCE (S256)
Scopes openid profile email and the scope for groups (often groups)
Groups must be in the signed ID token or in the UserInfo answer
The redirect URI is always APP_URL plus /api/auth/callback.

en.heading: Variables
paragraphs: APP_URL=https://flowplan.example.com
OIDC_ISSUER=https://id.example.com/realms/company
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=flowplan
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=secret
OIDC_SCOPES=openid profile email groups
OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM=groups
OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP=flowplan-admins
SESSION_HOURS=8
Variable Meaning
OIDC_ISSUER The issuer URL; Flowplan reads the discovery from it (/.well-known/openid-configuration).
OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM The claim with the groups, also as a path such as realm_access.roles.
OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP Members of this group see the Administration. The name is compared exactly.
OIDC_ALLOWED_GROUP If set, only members of this group may sign in.

OIDC_LINKED_SSO_ONLY true: accounts connected to SSO sign in through SSO only (off by default). A password or passkey sign-in is refused with a note; passkeys and the authenticator app stay for confirming important steps. See Connect an existing account to SSO.

OIDC_NEW_ACCOUNTS false: SSO sign-in creates no new accounts (on by default) – only existing, connected or SCIM-provisioned accounts sign in. At a first SSO sign-in with a known address, "Create a separate account instead" is then not offered.
OIDC_PROMPT_CREATE true: Sign up opens the provider's registration directly (prompt=create).

OIDC_PICTURE Take the profile picture from the picture claim (on by default, off turns it off). The image must be at a public HTTPS address; internal addresses are not fetched – not even via redirects.
SESSION_HOURS How long a browser session is valid in hours, as long as "Stay signed in" is not used; the apps stay signed in (see Stay signed in).

en.heading: Group names with common providers
paragraphs: – Keycloak: add the "Group Membership" mapper to the client, token claim name groups, turn off "Full group path" – otherwise the group is called /flowplan-admins. For realm roles use OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM=realm_access.roles instead.

– Authentik: the profile scope already delivers groups with the group names – a scope groups is not needed. The issuer is the provider's address with the trailing slash, e.g. https://auth.example.org/application/o/flowplan/. Without a signing key on the provider Authentik signs the ID token with the client secret (HS256); Flowplan accepts that from version 0.8.3 on. With a signing key (RS256) Flowplan also checks the signature against the provider's published keys. When you create the OAuth2 provider through the API, set grant_types explicitly to ["authorization_code"] (plus "refresh_token" if tokens should be refreshed): without it, Authentik 2026.8 gives it an empty list, and every sign-in fails with invalid_request ("The request is otherwise malformed"), which doesn't point at the cause.
– Zitadel: roles are under urn:zitadel:iam:org:project:roles; create a claim of your own with an action or enter the path.
– Entra ID: configure the groups claim in the token. Entra delivers object IDs by default; then enter the admin group's ID as OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP.

en.heading: When SSO sign-in fails
paragraphs: The server log names the reason: a line OIDC sign-in failed: with the kind of error, its code and – if the provider answered with an error – its error and error_description (never tokens or secrets). Common causes:

– Redirect URI: the provider must allow exactly /api/auth/callback. APP_URL has to be the address in the browser – otherwise the provider rejects the redirect or the sign-in cookie is missing ("Sign-in expired").
– Issuer: OIDC_ISSUER must match the issuer in the provider's discovery character for character, including a trailing slash.
– Client secret wrong, or a secret set for a client the provider treats as public (or none for a confidential one): the token endpoint answers invalid_client.
– unexpected JWT "alg": the provider signs ID tokens with another algorithm than it announces in its discovery.

en.heading: Connect an existing account to SSO
paragraphs: An account can sign in several ways: with e-mail and password, through LDAP and through one or more SSO identities (OIDC). Whoever created a local account first and gets SSO later connects the two – instead of ending up with a second profile.

From the settings: Under Settings → Account & security → Sign-in methods, choose Connect SSO …, confirm with your password, a code from the authenticator app or a passkey, then sign in with the provider. From then on the SSO identity (provider and subject) belongs to your account; you sign in with either. The flow only works for your account and the session you started it in, for ten minutes.
– If the SSO identity already belongs to another Flowplan account, nothing is connected. Ask the administrators to merge the two accounts.
– Disconnect (bin next to the SSO identity) works only while another sign-in method remains: a password, LDAP or another SSO identity.

– Remove password … is offered once an SSO identity is connected: you then sign in through SSO only. Passkeys and the authenticator app stay for confirming important steps. Set password … gives the account a password again at any time.

– Connecting, disconnecting and removing or setting the password are confirmed each time – with the password, a code from the app or a passkey. An account without any of these (SSO only) confirms with a sign-in at most ten minutes ago.

At the first SSO sign-in: When an SSO identity signs in for the first time, its provider has verified its e-mail address (email_verified), and exactly one Flowplan account with that address signs in with a password, LDAP or a passkey, Flowplan does not create a new account. A page asks instead: "An account with this e-mail already exists – connect it?" You confirm the existing account with its password (plus the code from the app when it is turned on) or its passkey; then both are connected and you are signed in. Create a separate account instead is offered only when the instance allows new SSO accounts (see OIDC_NEW_ACCOUNTS under Configuration). Nothing is ever connected without that proof; wrong passwords and codes count towards the lockout after too many attempts, as at a normal sign-in.
Good to know:
– A connected account with e-mail and password keeps its name, picture and admin right; SSO group mappings still do not change its memberships.

– With OIDC_LINKED_SSO_ONLY=true, connected accounts sign in through SSO only – a password or passkey sign-in then gets a clear note to choose "Sign in with SSO". Passkeys and the app stay for confirming steps.
– Connecting, disconnecting, refused connections, removing the password and merges are recorded in the security log (Administration → Security).
– LDAP accounts stay linked by their DN; they can connect SSO the same way (proof with the directory password). The LDAP link itself cannot be disconnected.
– When connecting, Flowplan asks the provider with prompt=login, so an account still signed in there is not connected by accident.
– With OIDC_ALLOWED_GROUP, only SSO identities in that group can be connected – as for signing in.

en.heading: Map SSO groups to workspaces
paragraphs: Groups from the identity provider (the claim in OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM) can give membership and groups in workspaces – so you manage access centrally in the provider.
– Admins map groups – for any workspace centrally under Administration → Sign-in & SSO → Map SSO groups centrally, or, where they are owners, under Settings → Groups & permissions → SSO groups.

– Owners who aren't admins see their workspace's mappings there but can't change them. A mapping brings people of the whole instance into a workspace and shows their addresses there – that is the administration's decision.
– A mapping gives a role (View, Edit, Owner), a workspace group (for page permissions) or both.
At every SSO sign-in Flowplan applies them:
– Matching people are added; with several matching groups the highest role wins. Guests stay at "Edit" at most.
– Whoever no longer has the SSO group loses what the mapping gave.

– The mapping always wins. If a mapping matches a person, Flowplan sets the role and groups to what the mapping says – even if the member was added or changed by hand. From then on the membership is managed through SSO.
– Members and group memberships that no mapping matches and that never came from SSO stay untouched.
– The last owner of a workspace always stays.
– Changed mappings apply right away to everyone with an active SSO session, otherwise at the next sign-in (with "Stay signed in" and SESSION_GROUPS_HOURS set, at the latest after that).
– Accounts with e-mail and password are not affected.

Note: changes by hand while SSO is active. If an owner changes the role or a group of a member who comes from an SSO group (marked "via SSO group …" in the member list), the change lasts only until that person's next SSO sign-in or the next change of the mappings. Then the mapping sets the role and groups again. Flowplan says so right after the change. For a lasting difference, the administration changes the mapping – or the person's groups in the identity provider.
In the member list and the group dialog, such members show "via SSO group “X”".

en.heading: User provisioning (SCIM)
paragraphs: With SCIM 2.0 your identity provider creates accounts in Flowplan, keeps name and address up to date and deactivates accounts as soon as someone leaves – without the person having to sign in first. Flowplan speaks SCIM 2.0 as in RFC 7643/7644 (users and groups, filters, PATCH).
Setting up
– Administration → Sign-in & SSO → SCIM tokens: Create token. The token starts with fpscim_ and is shown only once; only its hash is stored. You can revoke it at any time.
– At the provider, enter the SCIM base URL /api/scim/v2 and the token as bearer token.
– Assign people and groups to the app at the provider, or turn on "Push Groups".
What Flowplan does with it

– Accounts: a new SCIM account is an SSO account. If an account with the same e-mail address exists, it is linked instead of duplicated. At the first OIDC sign-in the person takes over the prepared account – by the externalId (= the provider's sub) or a verified e-mail address.

– Deactivating: active: false disables the account like Block in the administration – all sessions end at once, API tokens stop working. active: true enables it again. Deleting (DELETE) deactivates and unlinks; the content and the account itself stay, final deletion is still done in the administration. The last admin account with a password cannot be deactivated over SCIM.

– Groups: SCIM groups do not create groups in Flowplan. Their display name counts like an SSO group from the token: the SSO group mappings give the role and workspace groups, and all rules from there apply (the mapping always wins, the last owner stays). Membership changes take effect at once, not only at the next sign-in. A person's OIDC groups and SCIM groups are combined.
– Accounts with e-mail and password can be linked and deactivated, but mappings do not change their memberships.
– The last SCIM requests with their status are listed in the administration – useful when the provider reports errors.
Not supported: bulk, sorting, /Me and password changes (Flowplan stores no password for SCIM accounts).

en.heading: SCIM with common providers
paragraphs: – Okta: app integration (SAML or OIDC) → Provisioning → "SCIM connector base URL" = /api/scim/v2, "Unique identifier field for users" = userName, authentication mode HTTP Header with the token. Under "To App" turn on Create Users, Update User Attributes and Deactivate Users; add groups under Push Groups.

– Microsoft Entra ID: enterprise application → Provisioning → mode Automatic, "Tenant URL" = /api/scim/v2, "Secret Token" = the token, Test connection. Keep userPrincipalName → userName and objectId → externalId in the attribute mappings; set the scope to "Sync only assigned users and groups". Entra works in cycles of about 40 minutes.

– Authentik: Applications → Providers → create a SCIM provider, URL /api/scim/v2, enter the token; attach the provider to the Flowplan application as backchannel provider. Groups are sent with their names.
– Keycloak: Keycloak has no SCIM client of its own; install a SCIM extension (e.g. "keycloak-scim") or use LDAP or OIDC groups.

en.heading: Sign-in with LDAP
paragraphs: With LDAP_URL set, the password field of the sign-in page checks names against an LDAP directory (OpenLDAP, 389 DS, Active Directory, …). The field is then called E-mail address or user name.

– Accounts with e-mail and password keep signing in with their Flowplan password. Every other name is searched with the search account (LDAP_BIND_DN) and LDAP_USER_FILTER below LDAP_BASE_DN, and the password is checked by binding as that person. Empty passwords are never sent; the name is escaped as in RFC 4515, so * or ) in a name do not change the filter.

– An LDAP account is a directory account like an SSO account: the first time it is created by its DN or linked to an existing SSO/SCIM account with the same address. An account with e-mail and password of the same address is never taken over.

– Groups come from LDAP_GROUP_ATTRIBUTE (default memberOf): Flowplan takes the group's name (the first RDN, usually the CN, e.g. flowplan-admins) and the full DN. Either can be used in the SSO group mappings and as OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP.

– Hourly sync: Flowplan reads all LDAP accounts again – groups, name, address. Whoever is missing from the directory or locked there (Active Directory userAccountControl, 389 DS nsAccountLock, OpenLDAP ppolicy pwdAccountLockedTime) is disabled; once they are back, they are enabled again. Accounts disabled by an admin stay disabled. A run that would disable more than half of the accounts (at least five) stops – that is more likely a wrong configuration.
– Two-factor sign-in applies as for passwords: LDAP accounts can set up an authenticator app, and the instance's policy ("admins" or "everyone") applies to them too.
– Administration → Sign-in & SSO → LDAP directory shows the status, Test connection and Sync now with the last result.
Variable Default Meaning
LDAP_URL empty ldap://host:389 or ldaps://host:636. Without it, no LDAP.
LDAP_BIND_DN / LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD empty Search account. Without it, the search is anonymous.
LDAP_BASE_DN – Where people are searched, e.g. ou=people,dc=example,dc=org.
LDAP_USER_FILTER (\ (uid={user})(mail={user})) {user} is replaced by the escaped name. Active Directory: (\ (sAMAccountName={user})(userPrincipalName={user})(mail={user})).
LDAP_GROUP_ATTRIBUTE memberOf Attribute with the person's groups.
LDAP_TLS_CA empty CA certificate for ldaps:// or StartTLS (file path or PEM text). Certificates are always verified.
LDAP_STARTTLS false true: encrypt ldap:// with StartTLS.
LDAP_TIMEOUT_MS 8000 Time limit per LDAP operation.

en.heading: Examples
paragraphs: OpenLDAP (with the memberof overlay):
LDAP_URL=ldaps://ldap.example.org LDAP_BIND_DN=cn=flowplan,ou=services,dc=example,dc=org LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD=… LDAP_BASE_DN=ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
Active Directory:

LDAP_URL=ldaps://dc1.corp.example.com LDAP_BIND_DN=CN=svc-flowplan,OU=Service,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com LDAP_BASE_DN=OU=Staff,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com LDAP_USER_FILTER=(&(objectCategory=person)( (sAMAccountName={user})(userPrincipalName={user})(mail={user})))
Keycloak as the source: Keycloak itself is no LDAP server – connect Flowplan to the same directory Keycloak uses through "User Federation", or use OIDC.

Authentik: create an LDAP outpost (provider "LDAP", base DN e.g. dc=ldap,dc=goauthentik,dc=io), a service account with "Search full LDAP directory" as LDAP_BIND_DN (cn=,ou=users,), LDAP_USER_FILTER=( (cn={user})(mail={user})). Groups are in memberOf.

en.heading: Contacts from LDAP
paragraphs: Contacts databases import people from the directory and keep them in sync (directory → Flowplan only). Flowplan uses the server, search account and TLS of the LDAP sign-in (LDAP_URL, LDAP_BIND_DN/LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD, LDAP_TLS_CA, LDAP_STARTTLS, LDAP_TIMEOUT_MS). Base and filter can be separate:
Variable Default Meaning
LDAP_CONTACTS_BASE_DN LDAP_BASE_DN Where contacts are searched; the OU tree of the import dialog starts here. Entries outside it cannot be reached.
LDAP_CONTACTS_FILTER (&(\ (objectClass=inetOrgPerson)(objectClass=user)(objectClass=contact))(!(objectClass=computer))) Which entries are people.
LDAP_CONTACTS_SYNC_MINUTES 60 Interval of the sync (15–1440).
LDAP_CONTACTS_ATTRIBUTES – More attributes mappings may use (separated by commas or spaces). Without it only the attributes of the default mapping are allowed.
LDAP_CONTACTS on off turns contacts from the directory off.
For contacts alone, LDAP_URL with LDAP_CONTACTS_BASE_DN is enough; without LDAP_BASE_DN, sign-in with LDAP stays off.

Administration → Sign-in & SSO → Contacts from LDAP shows where base and filter come from and overrides them: base DN, filter, sync every … minutes, More attributes (attributes allowed on top of LDAP_CONTACTS_ATTRIBUTES, separated by commas) and Allowed (off: nobody can import, the sync rests). Stored values take precedence over the environment; empty fields fall back to the environment. Test connection checks the bind and the base. The search account's password stays in the environment and is never stored. Changes and imports are recorded as the security event “Security-relevant setting changed”.

Who may use the directory: instance administrators, accounts that sign in with LDAP and full members (not guests) of at least one workspace someone else created – never guests of the contacts database's workspace and never an API token. Someone with only workspaces of their own therefore cannot reach the directory, even though anyone may create workspaces. See Contacts from the LDAP directory.
Limits: at most 500 people per list in the dialog (search for more), 2000 linked contacts and 20 OUs per database; every operation has the LDAP_TIMEOUT_MS time limit.

en.heading: Stay signed in
paragraphs: How long a session lasts is set under Administration → Sign-in & SSO → Sessions (Administration); without a setting there, the environment variables and their defaults apply.
Where How long (default) Setting · variable
Browser without Stay signed in 8 hours after signing in – even while Flowplan is open Browser without “Stay signed in” · SESSION_HOURS (1–24)

Browser with Stay signed in 7 days after the last use, at most 30 days after signing in Offer “Stay signed in” in the browser · SESSION_REMEMBER (default off), Browser with “Stay signed in” · SESSION_IDLE_HOURS

Desktop and mobile app 90 days after the last use of the app or its widgets, at most 365 days after signing in Desktop and mobile apps · SESSION_APP_REMEMBER (default on), Apps: end without use · SESSION_APP_DAYS

– In the browser the sign-in page shows the Stay signed in box as soon as the administration offers it – for password, passkey and SSO (also through “Connect account”). It is meant for your own devices: when ticked, the session lives on while Flowplan is used. The longest lifetime (SESSION_MAX_DAYS, default 30 days, never shorter than the time without use) limits how long a stolen cookie is good for.

– The apps run on personal devices and always stay signed in – whether you signed in with a password in the app or with a passkey or SSO through the browser. The widgets keep the session alive as well. The app has to prove the sign-in is its own; that the app's name is in the user agent is not enough, because any browser can send it:
– Passkey, SSO or “Sign in in the browser”: the hand-off back to the app is the proof – only the app that started the sign-in can redeem it. This works with every app version.

– Password in the app: newer apps (iPhone, iPad and Android after 1.0.5, desktop after 1.3.0) create a random device key per server on first launch, keep it in the system's key store (Keychain, Android Keystore, the desktop's key store) and send it with the password. The first sign-in of an account on that device registers the key; later sign-ins need the same key. The server keeps only a hash.

– Older app versions (such as 1.0.5) have no device key: after a password sign-in they stay signed in like a browser – 8 hours, or with Stay signed in where the instance offers it (the box then appears in the app as well). Sign-ins with a passkey or SSO keep the app's lifetime; so do app sessions that existed before this change. An instance that does not want this sets Desktop and mobile apps to As in the browser without “Stay signed in” (SESSION_APP_REMEMBER=false). The app lock in the app's settings (Face ID, Touch ID, fingerprint or device passcode, on iPhone, iPad and Android) protects the phone further.

– SSO sessions extend the same way. Group changes at the provider follow through SCIM, the LDAP sync or the next sign-in. Only when SESSION_GROUPS_HOURS is set does an SSO session that stays signed in end after that many hours already: signing in at the provider again fetches the current groups, so OIDC_ALLOWED_GROUP and OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP apply by then at the latest, even without SCIM.
– A disabled account loses access immediately, as before.

– When the same person signs in again on a device (for example because the session ran out), the app's registration survives – notifications, widgets, Live Activities and Shortcuts move over to the new session. Only an explicit Sign out (in the app or under Signed-in devices) removes it.

– Shorter times apply from the next sign-in; longer ones extend sessions that stay signed in the next time they are used. Turning “Stay signed in” or the apps' staying signed in off stops the extending; running sessions then end at their next expiry.
Settings → Account & security → Signed-in devices lists all your own sessions with device, last use and end; Sign out ends a single one, Sign out all other devices all but the current one.

en.heading: Security check
paragraphs: Settings → Security check (/#settings/security) shows everyone how well their account is protected – tailored to how they sign in:

– The check: second factor, passkey and recovery codes left (e-mail accounts), a confirmed e-mail address, devices unused for over a month, API tokens without an end date or unused for three months, edit links without a password and end date, whether security notices arrive by push or e-mail, and failed sign-ins on your own account. Open points come first, each with the way to fix it. With SSO and LDAP it points to the provider or the directory.

– What you shared: your share links (with right and protection), public pages you created, and people or open invitations with their own access to your pages – each to delete, stop or remove right there.
– Sign-ins & changes of the last 30 days with device and network, including failed attempts with your address.
– Tips that fit the account.
When someone signs in with a device not seen for 90 days, a security notice arrives as well.

en.heading: Security
paragraphs: With OIDC, Flowplan checks the discovery, issuer, audience, signature, PKCE, state and nonce. Sessions are random tokens, stored hashed in SQLite; cookies are HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and Secure with HTTPS. Groups or roles are never taken from browser data.
– An account deactivated in the administration loses all sessions immediately; open live connections are closed within 15 seconds at the latest, as they are when read access is withdrawn.

– Every page carries a content security policy: scripts only run with a nonce that is new for every request, frames only come from the supported players (YouTube, Vimeo, Loom, Spotify, Figma, CodePen). The reverse proxy sets HSTS (usually active with Traefik/Coolify).
– Sessions can be revoked individually in the administration.
– Invitations to an e-mail address are only assigned after a sign-in with a confirmed address (email_verified=true with OIDC, the confirmation link for e-mail accounts).

en.heading: Common errors
paragraphs: Symptom Cause
An error about the redirect URI The URI entered at the provider does not exactly match APP_URL + /api/auth/callback.
No administration visible The group is missing in the token: check the scope, OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM and the exact group name, then sign in again.
"Invalid request origin" APP_URL differs from the address in use (e.g. http instead of https).
Sign-in refused OIDC_ALLOWED_GROUP is set and the person is not a member.
"Create account" is missing Sign-ups are closed: open them in the administration or invite the person.
A passkey cannot be created APP_URL is not an HTTPS domain (an IP address or http:// other than localhost).
How many people a Flowplan instance carries, what runs out first and what hardware to plan for small, medium and large teams – based on the load tests.

en.heading: Active people, not accounts
paragraphs: What matters is not how many accounts an instance has, but how many people work at the same moment: opening pages, typing, searching, changing records. An account that is doing nothing costs the server nothing.

The figures below count active people the way the load test simulates them: each sends a request every 1.5 seconds on average, or types continuously in a shared document. Real people read, think and switch to other apps – they create far less load. So the figures are a cautious limit: an instance that carries 20 such people copes with noticeably more real people signed in at the same time.

The administration shows how many are active at once on your instance: people active now on the overview and the Active people per hour chart under Administration → Monitoring (see Operations). Take the peaks, not the average.

en.heading: What one instance carries
paragraphs: Measured up to the first load step where things slow down: 95 % of reading requests above 500 ms, of writing requests above 1 s, or more than 1 % errors. "Carries" is the step before.
Setup Carries about Note
Single container with SQLite 20 active people One process, no other services
PostgreSQL, 1 instance with one dedicated core 30 active people Beyond that, read times rise steeply
PostgreSQL, 2 instances with one core each (cluster) 40–50 active people Still error-free at 60, but slow

The rule of thumb for planning: 25–30 active people per instance with one dedicated CPU core. For more people, add instances in cluster mode – this grows roughly linearly as long as PostgreSQL has headroom. An instance does its main work essentially on one core (Node.js); more cores per instance mostly help side work such as text recognition, more instances help with more people.
Measured on 4 vCPU (Intel Xeon, 2.1 GHz) with 16 GB RAM, PostgreSQL 16 and Redis 7 on the same machine. On a server running nothing else, and with faster cores, the figures are higher.

en.heading: What runs out first
paragraphs: – The instance's CPU – on reads: loading the sidebar with its permission checks page by page, opening large databases (all records) and search. These requests slow down first.

– Writes and live editing stay fast for long. At 60 active people on two instances, document changes (95 %) went through in 182 ms, and one person's change reached co-editors on the other instance through Redis in 195 ms.
– PostgreSQL was not the bottleneck in the test: writing requests stayed below 500 ms everywhere.

How you notice it in production: under Administration → Monitoring the response time (p95) rises, one core of the instance runs at full load all the time, and the System section shows connections "waiting".

en.heading: Recommendations
paragraphs: Guide values for people active at the same time at peak. Plan memory generously for imports, exports and text recognition of scanned PDFs.
Small Medium Large
Active at the same time up to about 20 about 20–60 more than 60

Setup one container with SQLite PostgreSQL, one container – from about 30 active people, or for updates without downtime, a cluster of 2–3 instances cluster with one instance per 25 active people, plus a spare
Flowplan 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM 1–2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM per instance 1–2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM per instance
Database SQLite on a local SSD (no NFS) PostgreSQL with 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, SSD PostgreSQL with 4+ vCPU, 8+ GB RAM, SSD, own server or managed service
Other services optional S3 in a cluster: Redis (small, no persistence), S3 Redis, S3

Database connections: set FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL to 10–20 per instance, and PostgreSQL's max_connections to at least instances × (FLOWPLAN_PG_POOL + 2) plus a reserve. Example: 4 instances with pool 20 need 88 connections; with a reserve, max_connections=150 fits.
Plan a spare: in a cluster, run at least one instance more than the load needs – during an update or when a node fails, the others carry on.

en.heading: Measure it yourself
paragraphs: The load tests are in the source code under scripts/loadtest: for a single container and for cluster mode (scripts/load-test-cluster.mjs, 1, 2 … instances against PostgreSQL and Redis). A measurement on the hardware Flowplan will run on tells you the most.

[!WARNING] Never measure against an instance people use: the test creates hundreds of accounts, pages and thousands of records and slows the instance down for everyone. Use a fresh, separate instance and delete it afterwards.
All data lives in one directory. With S3 storage, files are mirrored and the database is backed up continuously – the container then holds nothing irreplaceable anymore.

en.heading: What is where
paragraphs: Path in /app/data Content
flowplan.sqlite (+ -wal, -shm) All content, accounts, sessions, settings
uploads/ Uploaded files
web-push-keys.json Push keys, unless set via the environment
secrets.key Key for stored secrets, only without FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY and FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY (Configuration)
pre-restore-…, pre-move-… Previous state after a restore or a move; delete after a few days
ocr/ Language data for text recognition, recreated when needed

en.heading: Turn on S3 storage
paragraphs: With S3_BUCKET and credentials (see Configuration):

– Files: every uploaded file goes into the bucket right after saving, and deleted files move to /.deleted/uploads/ there; they are removed only once no kept scheduled backup in the bucket needs them, after one day at the earliest (delayed deletion). uploads/ stays the working copy. If a file is missing there – a new host, a lost volume –, Flowplan fetches it from the bucket: right away when requested, all others in the background.
– Database: Litestream transfers changes to the SQLite file to /db about every second. If the container starts without a database, Litestream first restores it from the bucket.

On the first start with S3, Flowplan uploads all existing files. Administration → Storage & backup shows the progress, the connection and the split between local and S3 (cards Backups and Usage); with FLOWPLAN_METRICS_TOKEN, or signed in as an administrator, /api/health shows it under objectStorage.pending.
MinIO, Garage, SeaweedFS, AWS S3 and other S3-compatible services are suitable.

en.heading: Garage
paragraphs: Garage creates neither the bucket nor the keys by itself:
garage status                                  # read the node ID
garage layout assign -z dc1 -c 10G <node ID>
garage layout apply --version 1
garage bucket create flowplan
garage key create flowplan
garage bucket allow --read --write --owner flowplan --key flowplan
garage key info flowplan --show-secret         # key ID and secret
S3_REGION must match the value s3_region in garage.toml.

en.heading: SeaweedFS
paragraphs: Start the S3 service so that it listens on all interfaces (-ip.bind=0.0.0.0), otherwise other containers cannot reach it. The endpoint is the S3 port, 8333 by default.

[!NOTE] Why no Postgres and no Redis by default? Flowplan works in one process directly on SQLite – faster and simpler for one instance per organisation. Sessions, presence and live sync run through the database and the process itself; Redis would have nothing to do. For larger teams there is PostgreSQL and cluster mode with Redis.

en.heading: Backups
paragraphs: – Instance backup in Flowplan (recommended): Administration → Storage & backup → Whole instance → Download downloads the database and files consistently while running.
– S3 with Litestream: a continuous backup; an earlier point in time can be restored (below).

– Scheduled backup: a consistent copy of the database every day or every hour, with S3 in the bucket under backups/, otherwise in the data folder – encrypted when a key is set (Encryption). Also to a server of your own via SFTP, with all files if you like, or through an SMB or NFS share. No scheduled backup is made before the first account exists (demo accounts and the development account do not count) – so a new instance does not put an empty copy next to the backups of an old one.
– A volume backup on the host or in Coolify. For a consistent copy, stop the container first.
– By hand while running:
sqlite3 /app/data/flowplan.sqlite "VACUUM INTO '/backup/flowplan.sqlite'"
Back up uploads/ and web-push-keys.json as well.
With PostgreSQL, scheduled backups and Back up now become pg_dump archives (flowplan-….dump) and Litestream is not used; targets, encryption and retention stay the same. See Backups with pg_dump.
The content archive under Settings → Import & export → Export → Workspace as ZIP backs up a workspace but does not replace an instance backup with accounts and permissions.

en.heading: Backup via SFTP
paragraphs: The scheduled backup can also go to a server of your own – a NAS, a backup server or rented storage with SSH access. Set it up under Administration → Storage & backup → SFTP target:

– Server, port (22) and user, sign-in with a password or a private key (OpenSSH or PEM, optionally with a passphrase). Flowplan stores password, key and passphrase only encrypted (stored secrets); afterwards the interface only shows that one is stored.
– Folder on the server: relative to the login folder or absolute (/srv/backups/flowplan); .. is not allowed. If it is missing, Flowplan creates it.
– Keep: this many backups stay in the folder, older ones are removed.

– Include files: mirrors the uploaded files to uploads/ in the folder. New files are added with every backup; files deleted for good in Flowplan move to .deleted/uploads/ (delayed deletion). Files the database still lists are never moved away there. If the uploads/ folder is missing or empty although the database lists files (a volume that is not mounted, say), the backup skips the mirror with an error; the database copy is still transferred.
– With FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, everything on the server is encrypted – the database as in S3 and the data folder (flowplan-….sqlite.enc), every file on its own (Encryption).

Host key: on the first Test connection, Flowplan shows the server's fingerprint (SHA256:…) before it sends any credentials. Compare it on the server with ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub and confirm it with Trust this key. If the server later presents another key (a reinstall – or someone intercepting the connection), every transfer stops and the administration shows the old and the new fingerprint; it only continues after Accept the new key. Another server or port always needs a new confirmation.

The SFTP backup runs with every scheduled backup (daily or hourly; Scheduled database backup must be on); Back up now in the SFTP target transfers right away. The last transfer and the last error are shown below it and in the status line at the top.
A restricted account on the server is enough, e.g. with OpenSSH:
Match User flowplan
ChrootDirectory /srv/sftp/flowplan
ForceCommand internal-sftp
AllowTcpForwarding no

en.heading: Delayed deletion
paragraphs: A kept backup should always be fully restorable – including the files deleted since it was made. That is why Flowplan does not remove deleted files on the SFTP server (with Include files) and in the S3 bucket right away:
– They move to .deleted/uploads/ (SFTP: in the folder, S3: under /). The time of the move is appended to the name (.), so it survives copying the folder or a restore on another instance.

– They are removed for good by a later backup once they were moved before the oldest backup still kept – then no backup needs them any more. In the bucket also not before one day has passed, as far as Litestream's history reaches back. So a higher Keep also means deleted files stay longer.
– If a deleted file comes back (after a restore, for example), the SFTP backup moves it back from .deleted/uploads/ instead of transferring it again.
– When restoring, Flowplan looks for a file missing from uploads/ in .deleted/uploads/.
Without scheduled backups (Scheduled database backup off), Flowplan deletes in the bucket right away – there is no backup that could need the file.

en.heading: SMB or NFS share
paragraphs: Flowplan does not speak SMB or NFS itself – the container would need mount privileges for that. Instead, Docker mounts the share as a volume, and the scheduled backup writes to the data folder's backups/ folder (the local target, i.e. without S3_BUCKET):
services:
flowplan:
volumes:
- flowplan-data:/app/data
# Put the share over the backups folder.
- nas-backups:/app/data/backups
volumes:
flowplan-data:
# SMB/CIFS (the Docker host needs cifs-utils)
nas-backups:
driver: local
driver_opts:
type: cifs
device: "//nas.example.lan/flowplan"
o: "username=flowplan,password=${NAS_PASSWORD},uid=1000,gid=1000,file_mode=0600,dir_mode=0700,vers=3.0"
For NFS instead:
nas-backups:
driver: local
driver_opts:
type: nfs
o: "addr=nas.example.lan,nfsvers=4,rw"
device: ":/export/flowplan"

uid=1000 is the user node Flowplan runs as; with NFS the export must be writable for this UID. The password comes from an .env file next to compose.yaml. In panels such as 1Panel or Portainer this is a "volume with driver local and options" or a "CIFS/NFS volume".

[!WARNING] Only put the backups/ folder on the share, never the whole data folder: SQLite needs reliable file locks, which SMB and NFS do not guarantee. The share only receives the database – for the files, download the instance backup or use the SFTP target with Include files.

en.heading: Encryption
paragraphs: On request, Flowplan encrypts everything it sends out of the server with a key only the server knows (AES-256-GCM). Whoever gets hold of the bucket or a backup – the storage provider, someone with leaked credentials, a bucket made public by mistake – sees only unreadable data.
What Encrypted
Files in the bucket (/uploads/) yes
Scheduled backups (flowplan-….sqlite.enc) yes, in the bucket and in the data folder
Markdown exports (….zip.enc) yes, in the bucket and in the data folder
Downloaded instance backup (….zip.enc) yes
Litestream replica of the database (/db/) no – see Litestream
Git export no – readable Markdown is what it is for
Data folder on the server (flowplan.sqlite, uploads/) no – use the host's disk encryption for that

en.heading: Turn it on
paragraphs: Create a key, set it as an environment variable and restart:
openssl rand -base64 32
# or without openssl:
docker run --rm ghcr.io/yannicschuller/flowplan node /app/decrypt.mjs --new-key
FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<32 bytes, base64>
# or as a Docker secret:
FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/flowplan-key

Administration → Encryption then shows “Encryption on” with the key ID (the first bytes of a hash, not the key itself). A malformed key shows up there as an error; backups then fail instead of being stored unencrypted.
[!CAUTION] Without the key, encrypted backups and files are lost – for you too. Keep it apart from the backups (password manager, vault), not in the same bucket and not only on the same server.

en.heading: Existing data
paragraphs: There is no migration step, and nothing is rewritten at startup. Flowplan recognises encrypted data by its first bytes, so unencrypted and encrypted data sit side by side without problems:
– From the moment you turn it on, new files and every new backup and export are encrypted.

– Files already in the bucket stay readable and unencrypted for now. Administration counts them; Encrypt existing objects uploads them once more in the background, this time encrypted, replacing the old object. The app keeps running normally meanwhile.
– Older backups and exports are not rewritten. Over time they drop out of retention (Backups kept), or you can delete them by hand.
– Restore works with both: an unencrypted instance backup can still be uploaded, and an encrypted one is decrypted first.
– If the bucket has versioning, older unencrypted versions of the objects remain. Remove them with a lifecycle rule or by hand.
Turning it off works too: move the key to FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS. Then nothing new is encrypted, but what is already encrypted stays readable.

en.heading: Change the key
paragraphs: – Set the new key as FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY and move the old one to FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS (several separated by commas), then restart.
– Under Administration → Encryption, choose Encrypt existing objects. All files in the bucket are re-encrypted with the new key.
– Keep the old key until the last backup encrypted with it has dropped out of retention.
Every encrypted file names the ID of its key. If that key is missing, Flowplan says exactly that instead of silently returning broken data.

en.heading: Litestream and encryption
paragraphs: Litestream (0.5) cannot encrypt the database replica itself. With a key set, Administration therefore warns that an unencrypted copy is kept under /db/. Two ways out:

– Encrypted backups only (recommended for a bucket you do not trust): set FLOWPLAN_LITESTREAM=off, turn on Hourly instead of daily under Administration → Storage & backup → Backups, and keep more copies (e.g. 72). Then delete the folder /db/ in the bucket. The price: in the worst case you lose the last hour instead of the last seconds, and on a new host you restore the database from the newest backup (below).

– Server-side encryption at the provider (SSE-C): set LITESTREAM_SSE_C_KEY to a key of its own (32 bytes, base64). The provider encrypts the replica and receives the key with every request to do so. That protects against leaked disks or buckets, not against the provider itself. It only works over https and only with providers that support SSE-C (check first). Empty the folder /db/ before turning it on, because a replica made of unencrypted and SSE-C parts cannot be restored.

en.heading: Emergency: decrypt without a running instance
paragraphs: decrypt.mjs needs only Node.js – no database and no running server. It is in the Docker image at /app/decrypt.mjs and in the source at scripts/decrypt.mjs:
# in the folder with the backup
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u)" -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work -e FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY='<key>' \
ghcr.io/yannicschuller/flowplan node /app/decrypt.mjs flowplan-2026-10-19-03-00.sqlite.enc
# → flowplan-2026-10-19-03-00.sqlite

The same works for Markdown exports (.zip.enc becomes .zip), for the instance backup and for single objects from uploads/ in the bucket (output .decrypted). Add earlier keys through FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS; --key-file reads the key from a file. The output only appears once the checksum is correct.
The format is openly documented: FPE1 (4 bytes) · key ID (8 bytes) · IV (12 bytes) · data · GCM tag (16 bytes). The first 12 bytes are authenticated as well.

en.heading: More protection
paragraphs: Encryption covers what leaves the server. On the server itself, the database and files are unencrypted, because Flowplan has to read them to show them. To cover that as well:
– Disk encryption on the host (LUKS, an encrypted volume at your provider). You can add it at any time, independently of Flowplan.
– The format carries a version (FPE1) and a key ID. A later switch to another method or key therefore goes the same way as above, without making old backups unreadable.
– Encrypting the running database (SQLCipher) is deliberately not part of this; see the reasoning in issue #32.

– For individual confidential content there are encrypted spaces: they are encrypted in the browser already, so the database, the uploads folder and the backups on the server hold only ciphertext – independently of FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

en.heading: Markdown export and Git
paragraphs: A readable copy outside Flowplan – for emergencies when the instance is down, or as an archive in a Git repository. Administration → Markdown & Git export chooses pages and databases; with every scheduled backup (and with Back up now) each becomes a Markdown ZIP with its sub-pages, comments and earlier versions:

– with S3 in the bucket under /exports/, otherwise in the data folder under exports/; as many are kept as backups (Backups kept). With FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY the ZIPs are encrypted (.zip.enc), the push to Git is not;
– the export reads with the permissions of the person who saved the selection – private records and journals with a PIN stay out;

– file names and paths in the ZIP contain ids, so they stay the same between runs (clean Git diff). Records start with YAML frontmatter, comments are in .comments.md, earlier versions under .versions/.

en.heading: Push into a Git repository
paragraphs: [!IMPORTANT] The instance Git export (EXPORT_GIT_*) is deprecated. It keeps working but is replaced by the Git export of a space, which space owners set up themselves; the administration shows a notice about it. The scheduled Markdown export to S3 or the data folder stays as it is.
With these variables Flowplan pushes every export into a repository itself (Forgejo, Gitea, GitHub, GitLab) – every page in a folder of its own, one commit per run with changes:
Variable Meaning
EXPORT_GIT_URL https:// address of the repository, without credentials.
EXPORT_GIT_TOKEN Token with write access to that repository. Only in the environment, never in the database or a backup.
EXPORT_GIT_USERNAME User name for the token (default flowplan; GitLab: oauth2).
EXPORT_GIT_BRANCH Branch, default main. An empty repository gets it on the first run.
EXPORT_GIT_AUTHOR, EXPORT_GIT_EMAIL Author of the commits.
EXPORT_GIT_IMPORT true: changes made in the repository since the last run are taken over before exporting.
With EXPORT_GIT_IMPORT=true, changed files are handled like this:
– Records (records//…md) are updated by flowplan.id in the frontmatter; new files become new records.
– Document pages (index.md, pages/…-.md) get the file's text; the previous state stays as a version.

– Journal days (/2026/10/2026-10-27.md) are found by their journal (the folder) and the date; flowplan.id in the frontmatter only counts when it names a day of the same journal. Repositories from older versions, where days were still pages/-.md, keep working: changes to those files are still taken over before the export, then the export writes the days to the new paths and removes the old files. No day is created twice; a renamed journal keeps its days because the folder is matched by its id.
– Database tables, comments and versions are copies and are not read back.

Markdown does not know every Flowplan block (such as columns). Whiteboards are in the repository as SVG images; an embedded board carries an invisible marker (``) that makes it an embed again when changes are taken over from Git – please leave the image and link below it in place. If you edit pages with other such blocks in Git, the previous state is in the version history. The administration shows the state of the last push (commit, changes taken over, errors).

en.heading: Git export of a space
paragraphs: Instead of one repository for the whole instance, the owner of a space sets up a repository for that space themselves: Manage space → Git export (via … next to the space or Settings → Spaces). The administration only switches the feature on:
Variable Default Meaning
SPACE_GIT_EXPORT empty true turns on the Git export of spaces. Without it, space owners don't see it and exports already set up don't run.
SPACE_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS empty Git servers, comma-separated, e.g. git.example.org,codeberg.org. When set, only these are allowed; without it, any public https:// server.

SPACE_GIT_ALLOW_PRIVATE empty true also allows internal addresses for the servers listed in SPACE_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS – for example a Forgejo on the same host that the container reaches via --add-host git.example.org:host-gateway. Only works together with the list; every other server stays limited to public addresses.
In the space, the owner enters:
– the repository address (https://, without credentials), branch (default main), user name and an access token with write access (GitLab: user name oauth2);
– the frequency: daily or weekly, plus Run now;
– optionally comments and earlier versions (.comments.md, .versions/).
What happens:

– The repository gets the Markdown export of the space – every top-level page in a folder of its own (-/), plus index.md and README.txt. Other files in the repository (such as LICENSE or CI files) stay untouched.
– One commit per run, and only when something changed; pages no longer in the space are deleted in the same commit.
– The export reads with the owner's permissions: private records of others and journals with a PIN stay out.
– Export only: Flowplan does not take over changes made in the repository.
– The settings show the last run (commit, files changed, error) and when the next one is due. A failed run is retried after an hour.
Security:

– Flowplan stores the token only encrypted (like the other stored secrets, bound to the space). After saving, the interface only shows whether one is stored; it is not in exports, and in the instance backup only encrypted. A new repository address needs the token again.

– Every address is resolved and checked: internal addresses (localhost, private networks) cannot be reached, redirects are not followed. The only exception: servers the administration lists in SPACE_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS when SPACE_GIT_ALLOW_PRIVATE=true is set as well – for example a Git server on the same host. Even then it stays HTTPS, with the pinned address and no redirects.

– The export ends, and token and working copy (git-export/spaces// in the data folder) are deleted, when the owner turns it off, leaves the workspace, becomes a guest or deletes their account – or when the space gets a new owner or moves to the trash.
Administration → Markdown & Git export shows how many spaces use the Git export and their last errors – without addresses or content.
